sens: The organ of the body in the mouth, instrument of speech and taste
A language or spoken tongue, a way of expressing oneself specific to a people
The miraculous gift of speaking in unknown tongues, a manifestation of the Holy Spirit
The word, what comes out of the mouth, considered morally
The ability to speak, verbal expression
An object shaped like a tongue
G1100.detail:
1. The tongue is primarily the physical organ in the mouth. Jesus touches the tongue of the mute to heal him (Mark 7:33), and the mute regains his ability to speak. It is the concrete instrument by which we speak.

2. A language is also an idiom, the way of speaking of a people or a nation. At Pentecost, each hears "speaking in his own language" the wonders of God (Acts 2:11): it is not the apostles who change their voices, but the people receive the preaching in their own language.

3. In Paul's epistles, "speaking in tongues" refers to a miraculous gift of the Holy Spirit: the believer speaks in an unknown language, which neither he nor the assembly usually understands (1 Corinthians 14:2). It is a visible manifestation of the gift of the Spirit (Acts 2:4, 10:46).

4. The tongue also symbolizes the word and what it produces. James forcefully reminds us: the tongue is "a fire," it "defiles the whole body" (James 3:6). It can bless or curse, hence the danger of misusing it.

5. To have a tongue is to be able to speak, to express what one thinks. This is why Pentecost changes everything: the apostles "receive" the word with boldness and clarity (Acts 2:4).

6. In Acts 2:3, the "tongues" that appear like fire are visual forms reminiscent of the human tongue, a living symbol of inspired speech.
G1100.origine: The Greek word γλῶσσα comes from an Indo-European root meaning what "shines" or what is "pointed," hence the tapered shape of the tongue. In Hebrew, the word לָשׁוֹן (lashon) has the same meaning. The Greek family also includes γλωσσάριον (small glossary) and the modern terms "glossary" or "glosse" (explanation of an ancient or rare word), which directly descend from it. This link from classical Greek to modern French shows how this word has served to describe speech and the interpretation of language.
G1100.emploi: The word γλῶσσα appears 47 times in the New Testament. In the Synoptics (Mark, Luke), it refers to the physical organ: Jesus heals the mute by acting on their tongue (Mark 7:33, 35; Luke 1:64). In Acts, the word shifts: after Pentecost, the apostles speak in foreign languages without having learned them (Acts 2:4, 11), and this gift is repeated in Caesarea (Acts 10:46) and Ephesus (Acts 19:6). Saint Paul, in his epistles to the Corinthians, extensively discusses the "gift of tongues" (1 Corinthians 12:10, 28, 30), distinguishing this gift from prophecy and regulating its use in the assembly (1 Corinthians 14:2-39). James uses the word to urge mastery over one's tongue, a source of evil if uncontrolled (James 3:5-8). Revelation uses it in the plural to refer to all peoples and their languages, gathered around the throne (Revelation 5:9, 7:9, etc.).
G1100.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that speech is a power: it blesses or curses, it builds up or destroys. James warns that mastering one's tongue is a sign of spiritual maturity (James 3:2). But γλῶσσα also evokes the miracle of Pentecost: the Holy Spirit gives the disciples the boldness to testify, and even the extraordinary gift of speaking in foreign languages so that everyone can hear. It is a call to take our speech seriously, as an instrument of Christian testimony and a reflection of the presence of the Spirit.

sens: Box or chest intended to receive and store objects
Bag or container for keeping money
Common fund of a group
G1101.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a closed container — a box or chest — designed to protect valuable objects. In the Greek Old Testament, this same word translates the ark, the sacred chest of the temple (2 Chronicles 24:8), where offerings were deposited.

2. In the Gospels, it becomes a bag or purse for money. Judas held the disciples' purse (John 12:6 and 13:29): he was the one who kept the group's common funds and managed the received donations. This role conferred a form of power, which John emphasizes by noting that Judas was also the thief.

3. More broadly, the purse represents the common fund, the shared treasure of a community. It is the collective money available for the needs of the group — to feed the disciples, buy what is necessary, or help the poor.
G1101.origine: The Greek word combines two roots: "glôssa" (the tongue, the flap) and "komeo" (to carry, to hold). Originally, it referred to a case for the reeds or tongues of musical instruments — small valuable objects that needed protection. Gradually, the term expanded to any container intended to hold valuable things, especially money. The word has simplified over time, shifting from the longer classical form to the shorter form of the New Testament.
G1101.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, in the two places where the Gospel of John discusses Judas's role. In John 12:6, John reveals to the reader that Judas, who held the purse, was stealing its contents — an act that betrays his love of money. In John 13:29, the other disciples, unaware of Judas's betrayal, simply think that Jesus is entrusting him with a task related to his role: to buy food for the Passover feast or to give to the poor. The purse thus embodies the administrative service and material stewardship of the apostolic group, but also — in Judas's case — the temptation of embezzlement.
G1101.portee: This word reminds us that even within the group of apostles, the management of money could be a spiritual issue. Judas had access to the common fund, a responsibility entrusted to him by Jesus, but he betrayed it. This invites us to reflect on our faithfulness in small things — how we manage what is entrusted to us, how money can become a temptation, and how selfless service is at the heart of the Christian life.

sens: Craftsman who cleans and whitens woolen fabrics
One who prepares fabrics by washing, carding, and pressing
By extension, one who makes something white and bright
G1102.detail: 1. A foulon is a craftsman specialized in cleaning and whitening fabrics, particularly wool. He uses physical and chemical processes to remove impurities, card the fibers, and give the fabric its whiteness and brightness. In Mark 9:3, when the Gospel describes the garments of the transfigured Christ, it compares them to a whiteness that no foulon on earth could match, showing that supernatural purity surpasses the best human techniques. 2. The foulon first carded the wool to prepare it, then washed it with ancient cleaning products, before pressing and stretching it to give it shape and shine. 3. By extension, the word evokes the idea of purification and transformation: making something white, pure, and radiant by deeply cleaning it.
G1102.origine: The Greek word comes from the verb κνάπτω ("to card wool"), which describes the initial gesture of the foulon: combing the fibers to untangle and prepare them. It is an ancient profession, attested in both Greece and Israel. The Hebrew כָּבַס ("to wash") designates the same profession, and the Septuagint translates this Hebrew term as γναφεύς in the account of the siege of Jerusalem (Isaiah 7:3, 36:2), showing that the foulon was a well-known figure in the ancient world.
G1102.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Mark 9:3, during the Transfiguration of Jesus. Matthew and Luke use a slightly different formulation, but the idea remains: the whiteness of Christ's garments is so extraordinary that no human technique could match it. The foulon, a figure of the best cleaning and whitening craftsman known to ancient readers, serves as a standard of comparison to emphasize the supernatural nature of the scene.
G1102.portee: This word sheds light on the Transfiguration: it is not a work of human art or cosmetics, but a manifestation of divine glory that infinitely surpasses human capabilities. For the Christian, it reminds us that only Christ can truly "whiten" our sins (cf. Isaiah 1:18) and transform us deeply — no earthly purification or human effort is sufficient.

sens: Truly authentic, without pretense
Who is truly a legitimate child, born of marriage
True, devoid of duplicity or falsehood
G1103.detail:
1. Sincere means what is truly authentic and straightforward. When Paul speaks of the "sincerity" of the Corinthians' love (2 Corinthians 8:8), he refers to genuine love, without artifice or hidden motives. It is the opposite of feigned or deceptive appearances.
2. Originally, the word evokes the child truly born of marriage, thus the legitimate son or daughter of a father. Paul applies this image to his relationship with Timothy and Titus, calling them his "legitimate children in the faith" (1 Timothy 1:2, Titus 1:4): he means that they are his true disciples, born of his teaching, not merely nominal disciples.
3. The word also carries the idea of fidelity and constant loyalty. When he calls his coworker "faithful" in Philippians 4:3, Paul designates someone in whom one can trust, who remains true in the fight for the Gospel.
G1103.origine: The word comes from the Greek root γίγνομαι (gignesthai), which means "to be born" or "to beget." Gnésios thus primarily designates what is well-begotten, legitimate — a child born in marriage, as opposed to a bastard. This image of the true-born has extended to the moral sense: what is true, unmingled, authentic. It is a word from the family of genos (race, origin).
G1103.emploi: Paul uses this word four times in the New Testament, always to qualify relationships or feelings essential to Christian life. Twice he uses it to refer to his disciples: Timothy and Titus are his "legitimate children in the faith," meaning that he himself trained them in the Gospel and can recognize them as true spiritual sons (1 Timothy 1:2, Titus 1:4). Once he qualifies a coworker as "faithful" (Philippians 4:3), emphasizing his constancy and dedication. Finally, in 2 Corinthians 8:8, the word becomes a noun to designate the "sincerity" of charity, that is, its moral authenticity.
G1103.portee: This word reminds us that the Christian faith does not tolerate duplicity: it demands sincerity of heart, an authenticity that God discerns. For the reader, it underscores the importance of faithfully transmitting the Gospel from teacher to disciple, and the seriousness with which Christians must engage. It is an invitation to true faith, not to falsehood.

sens: with honesty and loyalty of heart
without ulterior motives or falsehood
with honesty and authenticity in feelings
G1104.detail: 1. Sincerely means in an honest and straightforward manner, without pretense or lies: one acts with transparency, saying or showing what one truly thinks. 2. It also means to act without ulterior motives, without seeking to deceive or manipulate: one genuinely cares for the well-being of others, not just for one's own advantage. In Philippians 2:20, Paul seeks someone who "sincerely" cares for the welfare of the Philippians, meaning someone whose heart is genuinely and selflessly turned toward them.
G1104.origine: The word comes from a Greek root that refers to what is authentic and true, particularly in familial or affectionate bonds. The adverb retains this idea of authenticity: to act sincerely is to act as one truly thinks, without a mask.
G1104.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Philippians 2:20. Paul speaks of Timothy, saying that he will "sincerely" care for the well-being of the Philippians. It is a rare but precise term to designate a form of devotion that is not feigned, an honest concern for the well-being of others. Its use emphasizes that Timothy is not seeking his own interest, but the true spiritual prosperity of the church.
G1104.portee: For the Christian, this word invites an examination of the heart: are our actions for others sincere, or do they hide selfish calculations? Paul praises Timothy because he genuinely cares for the Church, without pretense. It is a call to transparency and authenticity in our fraternal relationships.

sens: Thick darkness, cloud or dark mist
Atmosphere of storm and chaos
Image of the fearsome presence of God
G1105.detail:
1. The word designates a dense and palpable darkness, like fog or a thick cloud that envelops and obscures everything. In Hebrews 12:18, Paul evokes the "cloud" of darkness that surrounded Mount Sinai during the revelation of the Law — a darkness so thick that one could not see.
2. This darkness carries with it a dimension of storm and chaos: it is not merely the absence of light, but a threatening, agitated element that inspires fear and trembling. The cloud of Sinai was accompanied by flashes of lightning, thunder, and the roar of the storm.
3. In the biblical context, this cloud represents the mysterious and fearsome presence of God — a God who manifests Himself in power and judgment, hidden from sight, inaccessible to touch, imposing respect and reverence rather than familiarity.
G1105.origine: The Greek word gnophos comes from an ancient form and evokes the idea of something that envelops and obscures. In the Septuagint, it translates Hebrew words like aphel ("darkness") and araphel ("mist"), which describe mysterious and sacred darkness. This word belongs to the same family as other Greek terms for darkness and gloom, but with the particular nuance of something palpable and threatening.
G1105.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: in Hebrews 12:18. The author uses it to contrast the ancient revelation of Sinai — marked by terror, fire, and impenetrable cloud — with the new revelation in Jesus Christ. Paul paints a dramatic scene of a mountain surrounded by thick darkness and a storm, to show how believers are no longer subjected to this terrifying revelation, but to a direct and confident approach to God.
G1105.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that the Old Testament revealed a holy and terrible God, whose presence was surrounded by mystery and dread. But for the Christian, this revelation has given way to a direct and loving relationship with God through Jesus Christ — no longer paralyzing fear, but trust and filial access.

sens: what one thinks, one's personal opinion
what one intends to do, one's resolution
the advice given to someone
the decision, decree of an authority
G1106.detail:
1. An opinion is primarily what one thinks, one's own judgment or feeling about a matter. Paul asks the Corinthians to be "perfectly united in the same mind" (1 Corinthians 1:10): this refers to sharing the same conviction, the same point of view.
2. It is also what one has resolved to do, an intention or personal decision. In Acts 20:3, Paul "decided" (the Greek word refers to his opinion, his resolution) to return to Macedonia rather than embark for Syria.
3. An opinion can be the advice given to others. Paul says: "I give my opinion, as one who has received mercy from the Lord" (1 Corinthians 7:25); he offers his informed judgment, not a mandatory command. In Philemon 1:14, Paul wants the master to act "without advice" (that is, without external pressure).
4. Finally, an opinion can be the official decision of an authority: in Revelation 17:17, it refers to the royal "purpose," the decree that God will implement.
G1106.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "to know" (gnōskō). An opinion is therefore initially what arises from knowledge, what one knows and thinks about it. In Hebrew, there was a similar word (taam) that referred to taste, judgment, and the order of a king. It is a word that circulates widely in classical Greek authors to designate the operations of the mind: to understand, to judge, to decide.
G1106.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul's epistles. In 1 Corinthians, Paul uses it to give advice fraternally, clearly distinguishing his personal opinion from the Lord's command (1 Corinthians 7:25, 40). In 2 Corinthians 8:10, it is a kind recommendation about generosity. In Philemon 1:14, the opinion is what is requested out of respect. Acts 20:3 shows the opinion as a decision, a resolution that one makes. In Revelation 17:13 and 17:17, the opinion takes on a solemn dimension: it is the divine or royal purpose that will be fulfilled.
G1106.portee: This word teaches us that true spiritual authority is never imposed harshly: Paul gives opinions, consults, and seeks consent. There is an important distinction between a mandatory command from the Lord and the wise counsel of a pastor or an elder brother. For the Christian, it is a call to seek unanimity in faith, to respect the opinions of those filled with the Holy Spirit, and to do nothing that contradicts one's conscience or that of others.

sens: To learn something, to discover through experience or information
To reveal, intentionally communicate information to someone
To manifest or publicly show what was hidden
G1107.detail:
1. The verb primarily means to learn or discover — to move from ignorance to knowledge. This meaning is seen when Ephesians 3:3 speaks of the "knowledge of the mystery": Paul discovered the divine secret that was revealed to him, and he became aware of it.

2. More often, the word means to transmit information, to ensure that someone learns something. John 17:26 illustrates this: Jesus "made known" the name of the Father to the disciples — he communicated it, revealed it. Similarly, in Philippians 4:6, we must "make known" our needs to God through prayer — that is, express them to Him.

3. The word also carries the idea of publicly manifesting, making visible what was invisible. In Romans 9:23, God wants to "make known" the riches of His glory — He wants to show it, reveal it to the world through His acts. It is an act of intentional, voluntary revelation.
G1107.origine: The word comes from the same root as γιγνώσκω (to know), but with a prefix that adds the idea of "to inform" or "to make known." Originally, it expresses the transition from secret to revelation, from hidden to manifest. It is an active verb: someone passes knowledge to another or discovers something for themselves.
G1107.emploi: The verb γνωρίζω appears 23 times in the provided New Testament passages. It has two main connotations. First, it can refer to the simple act of learning or becoming aware (Ephesians 3:3). But it is mostly used in the sense of communicating, transmitting — particularly when it comes to divine revelation: God or His messengers "make known" to humans His wills, His mysteries, His glory (Romans 9:22-23, Ephesians 1:9, 6:19). Paul also reports how he makes known the Gospel (Ephesians 6:19), how Jesus made known the name of the Father (John 17:26), or how the shepherds told what they had heard (Luke 2:15). It is a verb of revelation and communication, often in a serious spiritual context.
G1107.portee: This word reminds us that the Christian faith is based on communicated knowledge — we do not discover God by our own strength, but He "makes Himself known" to us through His revelation, through the Gospel, through the Spirit. It also emphasizes our freedom and responsibility to share: making known the Gospel, revealing the name of the Father, is the role of the believer as well as that of the apostle. Finally, the word suggests that certain divine truths remain hidden until God reveals them — mysteries that require His revelation to be known.

sens: the act of seeking to know, investigation
what one knows, acquired knowledge
intimate understanding of a person or spiritual truth
knowledge of God and His salvation revealed by the Gospel
Christian understanding capable of discerning good and evil
G1108.detail:
1. In its primary sense, it is the act of seeking to understand, to investigate — but this sense is rare in the New Testament.

2. More often, it is simply what one knows, the knowledge one possesses. Paul writes to the Romans that they are "filled with all knowledge" (Romans 15:14), meaning they have received solid Christian instruction and the ability to judge matters.

3. Knowledge is also an intimate and personal understanding. When Paul speaks of knowing the love of Christ "that surpasses all knowledge" (Ephesians 3:19), it is not merely intellectual knowledge, but a heart-transforming experience, an intimacy with Christ that surpasses all that can be learned through reason.

4. Knowledge takes on particular importance when it concerns God and salvation. Luke 1:77 speaks of the "knowledge of salvation" — it is the personal knowledge, by faith, that God forgives our sins. It is the fruit of the Gospel.

5. Finally, knowledge can refer to spiritual discernment that guides the moral conduct of the believer, particularly in matters of conscience — as when Paul addresses the issue of meat sacrificed to idols (1 Corinthians 8:10 and following), where knowledge without love risks hurting the weak.
G1108.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "to know" (γιγνώσκω). It denotes not the act of seeing something once, but the result of seeking to know, of gradually acquiring understanding. In the Greek Old Testament, it primarily translates the Hebrew "daath," which evokes both knowledge and intimate experience. The root suggests a knowledge that engages the person, not a mere recording of information.
G1108.emploi: The word appears 28 times in the New Testament, heavily concentrated in Paul's letters. Paul values Christian knowledge as a gift from God and part of the believer's maturity (1 Corinthians 1:5; Romans 15:14). But he also warns of its dangers: knowledge alone, without love, loses sight of Christ (1 Corinthians 13:8, where it "will pass away"); it can also be the subject of false teachings (1 Timothy 6:20, "false knowledge"). Biblical knowledge always aims at a relationship with God and Christ, never a purely theoretical understanding. It is a gift mentioned among the charisms (1 Corinthians 12:8).
G1108.portee: For the Christian, this entry reminds us that knowing God is not a matter of pure intelligence, but of heart and life. The knowledge that the Bible aims for is transformative and personal — it is learning to know Jesus Christ Himself. It should never turn into pride or judgment of the weak (1 Corinthians 8), but should be accompanied by love and wisdom. Thus, it truly becomes a spiritual wealth.

sens: one who has a deep and practical knowledge of something
an expert, a specialist
G1109.detail:
1. The word designates someone who knows a field well — not a distant theoretical knowledge, but a lived, in-depth understanding. In Acts 26:3, Paul addresses King Agrippa by recognizing him as a "connoisseur" of Jewish customs and discussions: he has grown up among them, understands them from the inside, and knows the nuances of their debates.
2. Thus, he is an expert, someone you can trust because he truly masters his subject. Paul cleverly flatters the king by calling him this, suggesting that he is worthy of listening to a man who, like him, possesses an intimate knowledge of these realities.
G1109.origine: The word comes from the root "to know" (γιγνώσκω) with the suffix -της which creates an agent noun: one who knows. In Hebrew, the Greek Old Testament often uses the word יִדְּעֹנִי (one who knows) to express someone who possesses experimental and reliable knowledge of something.
G1109.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 26:3. Paul uses it to court King Agrippa before pleading his case: recognizing in him an expert on Jewish realities shows him respect and encourages listening, while creating a complicity that should predispose him to a favorable hearing. It is a noble word, implying rich experience and recognized authority.
G1109.portee: This word reminds us that true knowledge is not an accumulation of facts, but a living familiarity with reality. It is recognized in one who takes the time to listen, understand, and discern nuances. It is also a call to respect those who have cultivated deep knowledge — and to cultivate true knowledge ourselves, rooted in experience.

sens: That which is known, known by someone or the public
That which is an acquaintance, someone one frequents
What is notorious, manifest, remarkable
What is accessible to knowledge, intelligible
G1110.detail: 1. A fact, word, or person that has been learned or recognized: it is something that is not ignored, that has circulated and spread (Acts 9:42: the miracle of the resurrection of Tabitha "became known throughout all Joppa"). 2. A person one knows, whom one frequents regularly, an acquaintance in the sense of a personal relationship (Luke 2:44: Jesus as a child was among "his acquaintances" during the journey, meaning among those who regularly traveled with the family). 3. A sign or wonder that strikes, that is noticeable and cannot be ignored (Acts 4:16: "a notable sign" performed by the apostles, which no one can contest). 4. What can be perceived or understood by intelligence, what falls under the domain of knowledge (Romans 1:19: "what can be known about God" — even God's invisible qualities are accessible to human reason).
G1110.origine: The word comes from the root γιγνώσκω ("to know, to learn") and literally means "that which has been known". The adjective γνωστός designates what has undergone the action of knowing, hence "known". In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it regularly translates ידע (yada), which expresses both intellectual knowledge and relational knowledge (to know someone as a friend).
G1110.emploi: The word appears fifteen times in the New Testament, mainly in Acts and in the context of public proclamation. It first qualifies facts whose knowledge has spread: the miracle of Tabitha, the crucifixion of Christ, and his resurrection become "known" to all the people (Acts 1:19, 9:42, 4:10). It is also used to designate acquaintances, "known ones" in the sense of people one frequents (Luke 2:44, 23:49). In John 18:15-16, it qualifies a disciple "known" to the high priest, meaning there is a personal relationship, a closeness. Paul uses it more abstractly in Romans 1:19 to speak of what "can be known" about God, that is, what is epistemically accessible to human reason.
G1110.portee: This word reminds us that the Christian faith is not a matter of esotericism or secrecy: the acts of God and the person of Christ become publicly known, accessible to all, proclaimed to the face of the world. It also emphasizes that knowing God is not an incomprehensible mystery, but something that can be reached and is based on verifiable facts and manifest signs.

sens: To express discontent in a low voice, grumbling
To complain in a subdued and persistent manner
To contest or criticize by speaking among oneself
G1111.detail:
1. To murmur is to speak in a low voice in an annoyed or discontented manner. It is the noise of people grumbling: the vineyard workers "murmured" against the master who paid the same wage to all (Matthew 20:11). The word evokes this continuous grumbling, this rumor of protest that rises.
2. It is also to complain in a subdued and tenacious manner, without shouting but letting one's discontent be heard. The Pharisees "murmured" against Jesus who ate with tax collectors (Luke 5:30); the Jews "murmured" because he said he was the bread from heaven (John 6:41). The complaint does not explode; it lingers.
3. It is to contest, to criticize by speaking in a half-voice, often together: "Do not murmur among yourselves," Jesus commands his disciples (John 6:43). Discussions happen in corners, doubts are raised, without directly confronting the one who has spoken. The Pharisees "hear the crowd murmuring about him" (John 7:32).
G1111.origine: The Greek γογγύζω (gonguzō) imitates the sound of murmuring — it is an onomatopoeic word, sounding like what it designates. In Hebrew, the Old Testament uses לוּן (lûn) to express the subdued discontent of the Israelites in the desert. The common idea is that of a complaint that rises, persistent and subdued, like a buzzing of discontent.
G1111.emploi: The verb appears 7 times in the New Testament, concentrated mainly in John (5 occurrences) and in the Synoptics. It describes a characteristic act: the crowds and the disciples express their doubt or anger in a low voice. Matthew (20:11) shows it among the aggrieved workers; Luke (5:30) among the scandalized Pharisees; John (6:41, 6:43, 6:61, 7:32) among those who do not understand or do not want to believe Jesus' words. In 1 Corinthians 10:10, Paul reminds that the Israelites in the desert "murmured" against God — this murmuring was a sin (Numbers 14). The word always designates an act of contestation or unexpressed doubt, which ferments in secret.
G1111.portee: Murmuring reveals a wavering faith or a reluctant submission. It is doubt that speaks in a low voice, rebellion that does not dare to name itself. The Bible does not condemn honest questioning, but it warns against this murmuring that divides, poisons, and secretly challenges without seeking to truly understand. It is a call to transparency and trust rather than to subdued complaint.

sens: Muffled sound of confused voices, rumor
Suppressed complaint, grievance
Expression of discontent or doubt expressed in a low voice
G1112.detail:
1. The murmur is primarily a sound of confused voices circulating among a crowd: in Jerusalem, when Jesus teaches, there is a great murmur among the people who wonder who he really is (John 7:12). It is a rumor that spreads, lacking strength or clarity, but fills the atmosphere.
2. The murmur also refers to a complaint, a grievance expressed in a low voice, even secretly. In the early Church, Hellenistic believers murmur against the Hebrew apostles because their widows are overlooked in daily assistance (Acts 6:1): it is a protest made in whispers, without direct confrontation.
3. Finally, the murmur is the expression of an inner discontent, a muted resistance to an order or exhortation. Paul calls the Philippians to do all things without murmurs, meaning without expressing their doubt or grievance, even if quietly (Philippians 2:14).
G1112.origine: The Greek word γογγυσμός comes from a root imitating noise: gong, gong… like a buzzing or continuous murmur. This same root is found in the verb γογγύζω (to murmur). In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, this word primarily translates תְּלוּנָה (tlunà, complaint) and אָוֶן (avèn, vain, evil), terms that denote the people's grievance against God in the desert. It is a word that depicts noise, not a clear cry, but a reproachful whisper.
G1112.emploi: The word appears 4 times in the New Testament, always to describe a negative human murmur. In John 7:12, it refers to the rumor circulating about Jesus. In Acts 6:1, it describes the complaint of the Greek widows against the unjust treatment they receive. In Philippians 2:14 and 1 Peter 4:9, murmuring is forbidden: Christians must serve without secret grievance, without this muted protest. The word always carries a negative connotation: murmuring is a form of doubt, discontent, or rebellion that simmers without being openly expressed.
G1112.portee: The murmur reveals the hidden heart: it is the complaint that dares not be voiced aloud, but weighs on the community. For the Christian, the invitation to act without murmuring calls for an inner, sincere obedience, without hidden reluctance. It is a call to trust in God and to brotherly unity: murmuring divides, even if it remains secret, because it expresses an unacknowledged doubt.

sens: one who murmurs, who complains in a low and muffled voice
one who grumbles, who complains about their lot
one who criticizes secretly, through murmurs
G1113.detail:
1. A murmurer is someone who murmurs — that is, who speaks in a low and indistinct voice, like someone who complains or protests without daring to say it frankly. In Jude 1:16, murmurers are depicted as people who complain about their lot instead of accepting God's will.
2. The murmurer is by extension one who grumbles, who shows their discontent in a muffled manner. It is less about open anger than about muted rebellion: one complains without directly confronting those who annoy them.
3. In a broader sense, it is one who criticizes, judges, or contests through murmurs and complaints. The context of Jude shows that the murmurer not only complains but also walks according to their desires and admires people out of self-interest — in other words, they unite their muted rebellion with selfish behaviors.
G1113.origine: The word comes from the verb γογγύζω (gonguzô), "to murmur, to grumble," which imitates the sound of a complaint in a low voice — it is an onomatopoeic word that reproduces the very sound of murmuring. The suffix -ιστής (-istês) forms agent nouns, meaning those who do something habitually or characteristically. A murmurer is thus someone for whom murmuring is a habitual trait of character. The Greek translators of the Old Testament (Septuagint) used this verb to render words of complaint and protest against God.
G1113.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Jude 1:16. Jude uses it to describe a category of false believers or intruders in the Christian assembly. These murmurers are not presented in isolation: they are characterized by a series of vices. They complain about their lot, but behind this complaint lie other faults — carnal desires, pride in speech, and a form of social hypocrisy (they admire people out of self-interest). Thus, murmuring is a symptom of a divided, dissatisfied, rebellious heart.
G1113.portee: For the believer, this word highlights a subtle and common sin: the muted complaint, the discontent expressed through murmurs rather than through confident faith. Jude warns us that murmuring is never isolated — it is always accompanied by other sins, selfishness, and a walk according to the flesh. It is a call to examine our hearts: do we grumble against our lot, or do we confess our true concerns to God? Hidden complaint is merely an ill-digested rebellion.

sens: One who deceives through words or actions to appear as what he is not
Magician or sorcerer who claims to have supernatural powers
Charlatan who abuses the credulity of others
G1114.detail:
1. The word fundamentally designates someone who deceives others by falsely presenting themselves, claiming to be or have something they are not or do not have. In 2 Timothy 3:13, Paul warns that "evil men and impostors will proceed from bad to worse" — these are people who seduce through lies and manipulation.
2. The Greek word also evokes the magician or sorcerer, one who claims to exercise hidden or supernatural powers to impress and dominate others. It is a form of spiritual deception.
3. In a broader sense, the impostor is a charlatan: someone who abuses the trust and credulity of the people by promising what they cannot deliver, by assuming an authority or knowledge they do not possess.
G1114.origine: The Greek word comes from a root that evokes a cry, a complaint, hence the initial image of the magician who recites formulas or moans to impress their audience. It is someone who "plays a role" through words and gestures to deceive — an actor of lies. The related noun "trickery" (in English) translates into French as deception or imposture.
G1114.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Timothy 3:13. Paul uses it in his final warning to Timothy about the difficult times of the last days: "impostors" are among the characteristics of "evil men" who progress in evil. The apostle emphasizes that these deceivers mislead others while being themselves misled — their lies are a form of spiritual folly. This context shows that imposture is not limited to popular magic, but encompasses any false spiritual or moral pretense.
G1114.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader of the reality of spiritual deception: some present themselves with authority and conviction while being themselves misled. It is a warning to remain vigilant against those who promise spiritual shortcuts or who claim false legitimacy. The true disciple learns to discern the authenticity of faith by examining the fruit and humility, not by being seduced by appearance or the assurance of speech.

sens: Place where Jesus was crucified, near Jerusalem
Hill or place of the skull
G1115.detail:
1. Golgotha is the name of the place where Jesus was executed by crucifixion. It is located near Jerusalem, outside the city walls. The three evangelists who mention it (Matthew, Mark, and John) specify it by giving its interpretation: "place of the skull" (Matthew 27:33, Mark 15:22, John 19:17).
2. The name "Golgotha" comes from Aramaic and literally means "skull." It can be imagined that this place bore this nickname because its shape resembled a skull, or because skulls were visible there—given that it was a place of execution. It is here that the salvation of the world was accomplished through the sacrifice of Jesus Christ.
G1115.origine: Golgotha is an Aramaic word (גָּלְגָּלְתָּא) that corresponds to the Hebrew גֻּלְגֹּלֶת, literally "skull." This word anatomically designates the skull bone. The Septuagint (Greek translation of the Old Testament) translates this Hebrew term with the Greek word κρανίον (kranion, skull). The choice of the name "Golgotha" for this place of execution remains mysterious, but reflects the importance of the skull in the imagery of death and judgment at the time.
G1115.emploi: Golgotha appears only three times in the New Testament, all in the Passion narratives: Matthew 27:33, Mark 15:22, and John 19:17. In each passage, the evangelists note that it is an Aramaic name and immediately specify its meaning for their Greek or non-Hebrew readers: "place of the skull." This treatment of the name shows that the gospel is addressed to readers who do not speak Aramaic and that it is important for everyone to grasp the identity of this unique place in the history of salvation.
G1115.portee: Golgotha is the geographical symbol of the heart of the Gospel: it is the place where Jesus accomplished the redemption of humanity through his death on the cross. For the believer, this name evokes not primarily geography or archaeology, but the mystery of God's infinite love that was given for us. Meditating on Golgotha is to stand at the foot of the cross and realize that it is there, precisely, that our salvation was sealed.

sens: Ancient city of the plain of Jordan, destroyed by God for its sins
Symbol of divine judgment on sin and immorality
Figure of the eternal destruction reserved for the wicked
G1116.detail:
1. Gomorrah is one of the five cities of the plain of Jordan, mentioned in Genesis alongside Sodom. It was destroyed by fire from heaven due to the moral corruption of its inhabitants, particularly their sexual idolatry and unnatural practices (Jude 1:7).

2. The Bible uses Sodom and Gomorrah as a typical example of God's judgment: their ashes serve as a warning to the ungodly to come (2 Peter 2:6). When Jesus speaks of the cities that would reject his disciples, he compares them to Sodom and Gomorrah, insisting that the judgment on the final day will be even more severe for them (Matthew 10:15).

3. The fate of Gomorrah illustrates that sin inevitably provokes destruction. Paul cites this judgment to show that only God's grace spared a remnant in Israel (Romans 9:29), reminding that without divine intervention, any people is doomed to ruin.
G1116.origine: The Hebrew name עֲמֹרָה (Amora) likely means "submersion" or "heap," evoking the totality of its destruction. Gomorrah is the Greek equivalent of this Hebrew name. The two cities, Sodom and Gomorrah, are always mentioned together in Scripture to mark the extent and certainty of divine judgment against sexual sin and impiety.
G1116.emploi: Gomorrah appears in five passages in the New Testament, always alongside Sodom. It is first mentioned as an example of judgment in Jesus' teaching (Matthew 10:15, Mark 6:11). Paul mentions it to show that grace alone saved Israel from total destruction (Romans 9:29). The letters of Peter and Jude make it a symbol of the final condemnation of the wicked: their destroyed cities reduced to ashes become a warning of the eternal fire that awaits them (2 Peter 2:6, Jude 1:7). In every use, Gomorrah represents God's inevitable judgment on flagrant sin.
G1116.portee: Gomorrah reminds the Christian that serious sin does not go unpunished. It teaches that God's judgment is real and that sexual immorality in particular provokes his wrath. But also mentioned with grace (Romans 9:29), it encourages the believer to turn to God to escape this fate and to take seriously the call to holiness.

sens: Load of goods transported by a ship
Set of goods and products traded
G1117.detail:
1. The word refers to the totality of goods loaded onto a ship for transport and sale. In Acts 21:3, the ship bringing Paul to Jerusalem must unload its cargo at Tyre: this is the normal commercial practice of a merchant ship of the time.
2. In Revelation 18:11-12, the word expands to refer to the wealth that Babylon accumulates and trades: gold, silver, precious stones, fine fabrics, fragrant wood, ivory, marble. It is the concrete image of prosperous trade and material enrichment.
G1117.origine: The Greek word γόμος comes from the verb γέμω ("to fill"). A cargo is literally what fills a ship. In the Greek Old Testament, the word translates the Hebrew מַשָּׂא (massa), which also means "load" or "burden." This family of words always evokes the idea of what is carried or transported, loaded onto something.
G1117.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, all in contexts of maritime commerce. In Acts 21:3, it is a practical operation: the ship must fulfill its commercial work. In Revelation 18:11-12, the context is prophetic: the fall of Babylon the Great leads to the collapse of international trade, and no one buys the cargoes it trafficked. The detailed enumeration of goods underscores the extent of the trade on which this city depended, before its destruction.
G1117.portee: This word reminds the reader that earthly commerce is temporary and fragile. The vision in Revelation 18 teaches that wealth and luxury, even considerable, can disappear in an instant when God's judgment intervenes. This invites the believer not to place their trust in the accumulation of material goods, but in what lasts eternally.

sens: One who has given birth to a child, father or mother
The collective of a person's father and mother
One who is responsible for educating and providing for a child's needs
G1118.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to one who has given birth to a child — the father or the mother. This is the simplest and most common meaning. When Jesus says in Matthew 10:21 that "children will rise against their parents," he is speaking of those who have begotten them.
2. Often, the word is used in the plural to refer to both parents together, with father and mother forming a unit. Luke 2:41 illustrates this well: "The parents of Jesus went to Jerusalem every year." This refers to Mary and Joseph, united in this parental role.
3. The word can also emphasize the responsibility of parents toward their children — their duty as providers and educators. In 2 Corinthians 12:14, Paul reminds that "it is not the children who are to save up for their parents, but parents for their children," which shows that the parental relationship involves an obligation of material and moral support.
G1118.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb meaning "to beget" or "to be born." It literally designates one who has given birth. The family of this word encompasses the idea of generation and lineage. In the Greek version of the Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew words for "father" and "mother" (father, mother), showing that Greek seeks to unify under a single term the parental reality common to both parents.
G1118.emploi: The word appears 19 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and the letters of Paul. It is regularly found in the plural (the parents) and in the singular (each parent taken individually). In the Gospels, it appears during the presentation of Jesus (Luke 2:27, 41, 43), in the story of the paralytic (Mark 13:12), and in the account of the man born blind (John 9, several occurrences). Paul uses it to remind of the reciprocal duties between parents and children (Ephesians 6:1, Colossians 3:20), or to show that disobedience to parents is a sign of moral corruption (Romans 1:30, 2 Timothy 3:2). The word always emphasizes the bond of lineage and responsibility.
G1118.portee: This word reminds children of the respect and honor they owe to their parents — a fundamental biblical commandment. Conversely, it reminds parents that their role is not for their own interest, but for the well-being and education of their children. The New Testament elevates the parental relationship to a rank of moral and spiritual priority.

sens: joint of the leg, between thigh and tibia
to kneel down, to kneel (gesture of prayer)
to bend the knee before someone (gesture of submission or worship)
G1119.detail:
1. The knee is the joint of the lower limb that connects the thigh to the leg. It is a part of the physical body, as when we speak of strengthening weak knees (Hebrews 12:12).
2. To kneel down means to bend one's knees to kneel, a gesture that accompanies prayer and expresses humility before God. Jesus knelt to pray before his agony (Luke 22:41), Peter did so when he prayed for Tabitha (Acts 9:40), and it is an act of respect toward God.
3. To bend the knee means to fold one's knee or kneel before someone to pay homage or acknowledge their authority. This can be a sincere act of submission to Jesus (Romans 14:11, Philippians 2:10) or a mocking act, as when the soldiers knelt before Jesus in ridicule (Mark 15:19).
G1119.origine: The Greek word "knee" directly corresponds to the Hebrew word "berekh" (בְרֵכָה). This word already existed in ancient Mediterranean languages to designate this visible and functional joint of the body. The Hebrew "berekh" is also the origin of the verb "to bless," as blessing often accompanied a kneeling gesture.
G1119.emploi: The word "knee" appears about a dozen times in the New Testament, mainly in Acts and in the epistles. It primarily describes the physical action of kneeling to pray: Luke reports that Jesus, Stephen, and Peter knelt (Luke 22:41, Acts 7:60, Acts 9:40, Acts 20:36, Acts 21:5). It then evokes submission or homage paid to an authority: bending the knee before God or before Jesus becomes the biblical image of recognizing their lordship (Romans 14:11, Ephesians 3:14, Philippians 2:10). Finally, it can be used ironically or contemptuously, when one feigns respect to mock (Mark 15:19).
G1119.portee: Kneeling in the Bible is not just a simple physical posture: it is the body language that recognizes God's authority and the power of Christ. Seeing every knee bow before Jesus (Philippians 2:10) affirms that all creation, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, will ultimately submit to his lordship. For the believer, kneeling to pray is an act of humility and trust: one relinquishes their own strength to place themselves under God's protection and guidance. This is why this gesture occurs so often in decisive moments of faith: prayer, intercession, surrender to divine will.

sens: To fall or to get on one's knees
To prostrate oneself before someone in a sign of respect, supplication, or worship
G1120.detail:
1. To kneel means to get on one's knees, adopting a low position. It is a bodily gesture that expresses humility or veneration. When the soldiers kneel before Jesus in Matthew 27:29, they physically take this posture.
2. This gesture also means to submit to someone, to ask something of them with respect or urgency. The leper in Mark 1:40 throws himself on his knees before Jesus to plead for healing: it is an act of trust and humility toward the one in whom he hopes.
G1120.origine: The Greek word combines two ideas: γόνυ (gonu, the knee) and πίπτω (piptō, to fall or to throw oneself). The starting image is therefore literal: "to fall on one's knees." It is a compound that describes the action of the body rather than an abstraction, which makes the word very concrete and visible.
G1120.emploi: This verb appears four times in the New Testament, always in the Gospels (Matthew and Mark). It describes moments when people seek to honor Jesus or obtain his help. In Matthew 17:14 and Mark 1:40, supplicants kneel to implore his healing. In Mark 10:17, the rich young man kneels while asking a serious question about eternal life. In Matthew 27:29, the soldiers use it ironically and contemptuously, mocking Jesus. In all cases, the gesture underscores the importance of the moment and the relationship of the one kneeling to the one before whom they kneel.
G1120.portee: Kneeling reveals the attitude of the heart. It is an act that expresses dependence, trust, or recognition of the authority of the one before whom one prostrates. For the believer, this reminds us that coming to Jesus involves a posture of humility and sincerity, and that respect for the Lord encompasses both body and spirit.

sens: mark or character drawn by hand
written document
knowledge of the scriptures, instruction
literal meaning of a text, as opposed to its spiritual meaning
G1121.detail:
1. A letter is primarily a mark drawn, a character of the alphabet that is written by hand. Paul illustrates this in Galatians 6:11 when he asks the Galatians to see "with what large letters" he has written himself, to emphasize his message with authority.
2. A letter or a written document in general: a missive addressed to someone (Acts 28:21, where the Jews say they have received no letter from Judea against Paul), or a commercial note, like that of the manager in Luke 16:6, where Jesus reports that the master asks the debtor to write a note for a hundred measures of oil.
3. The scriptures in the sense of knowledge and instruction — the knowledge of sacred texts. When the Jews marvel at Jesus' knowledge in John 7:15, they ask this question: "How does he know the Scriptures, having never studied?" Having letters means possessing formal education.
4. The letter as opposed to the spirit: the literal, external, material meaning of a law or a writing, in contrast to its spiritual depth. In Romans 2:29 and 2 Corinthians 3:6, Paul insists: circumcision "according to the letter" is merely formal obedience, while "the letter kills, but the spirit gives life," because a mechanical submission to the law, without a transformation of the heart, does not save.
G1121.origine: The word comes from the verb "to write" (graphô). Graphô means to draw, to inscribe: gramma is therefore literally what is drawn or inscribed, especially in writing. In Hebrew, the Greek Old Testament translates terms like "sèpher" (the book, the written document) with this word. The word family includes terms like "graphein" (to write), "anagraphein" (to record), "epigraphein" (to inscribe on). The fundamental image is that of a visible mark, of what is engraved or drawn and can thus be preserved and transmitted.
G1121.emploi: The word appears 14 times in the provided New Testament usages. It first simply denotes a written mark (Galatians 6:11), then an administrative document or any written text (Luke 16:6, 16:7: commercial notes; Acts 28:21: a letter). It broadens to the general notion of knowledge and instruction related to sacred texts (John 7:15, Acts 26:24: "the letters"). But it is in the Pauline epistles, especially Romans and 2 Corinthians, that the meaning sharpens in theological contrast: the "letter" becomes the principle of the law observed mechanically, without access to the transformative power of the Holy Spirit. This contrast structures Pauline thought on the new covenant.
G1121.portee: For the Christian, this word reveals a crucial tension: Scripture, although inspired and true, only saves if it is received through the transformative action of the Holy Spirit. A purely formal obedience to the Law, knowledge of the texts without a living encounter with God, remains a dead letter. Jesus and Paul teach us that the heart must be transformed, not just the external action controlled. This distinction calls us to seek in Scripture not a law that we endure, but a word that the Spirit comes to enliven within us.

sens: state secretary or official in charge of administration
military officer responsible for records and archives
teacher of the Jewish law, expert in sacred Scripture and interpretation of the Torah
G1122.detail:
1. The scribe, originally, is a functionary who writes and keeps official records: he is an administrative agent of the state. In Acts 19:35, the clerk of Ephesus is called a scribe, as he manages the documents and administration of the city.
2. In the army, the scribe is an officer responsible for military records and personnel: he plays an administrative and documentary role in the armed forces.
3. In Israel, the scribe becomes primarily a religious teacher, a scholar who knows the Law of Moses and teaches it. In Matthew 7:29, Jesus speaks with authority, while the scribes teach the Law, but the people recognize a different power in Jesus. Matthew 23:2-29 shows the scribes and Pharisees as the official interpreters of the Law, which they guarded jealously and imposed rigorously.
G1122.origine: The word comes from the Greek "gramma" (letter, inscription, writing). The scribe is one who masters writing and reading. In the Greek of the Old Testament, this word translates the Hebrew "sopher" (one who counts, who writes), which first designates an administrative officer, then a teacher of the law. The same root produces "grammata" (the holy Scriptures) and "grammateus" (one who knows them, the expert).
G1122.emploi: The word appears 67 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke) and in Acts. The scribes are depicted as a class of teachers and religious leaders who interpret and apply the Law of Moses. Often associated with the Pharisees (Matthew 5:20) and the chief priests (Matthew 2:4, Mark 14:53), they are adversaries of Jesus, who contests their authority and teaching. Mark 1:22 contrasts the authority of Jesus with that of the scribes. Some scribes, however, recognize the wisdom of Jesus (Luke 20:39), and Matthew 13:52 mentions a scribe instructed in the Kingdom, a positive image that anticipates the Christian disciple.
G1122.portee: The scribe embodies the danger of knowledge of God without obedience of the heart: the scribes know the Scriptures but do not recognize the one of whom the Scriptures speak. Their example warns the Christian reader: intellectual mastery of the Word is not enough; only a living relationship with Jesus, based on faith and humility, grants authority and freedom. It is an invitation to listen to Jesus rather than to adhere to human interpretations, however scholarly they may be.

sens: That which has been drawn, engraved, or marked by writing
That which is fixed in writing, recorded in a document
Figuratively: inscribed, engraved in the mind or heart
G1123.detail:
1. The primary meaning is literal: something that has been painted or written, marked by characters or signs. It is the adjective that designates the result of the action of writing, like a law written on a tablet or a text on paper.
2. More broadly, it designates what is fixed in writing, permanently and officially recorded — as opposed to what is simply said or memorized. This implies authority and durability.
3. In a figurative and moral sense, Paul in Romans 2:15 speaks of the law "written" in the hearts of the Gentiles: he means that the knowledge of good and evil is engraved, inscribed deeply within them, just as the Ten Commandments were engraved on stone. It is a strong image: the moral law is as real and present in them as if it were traced in visible letters.
G1123.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "graphô" (to write, to draw, to paint). The root evokes the action of marking a surface — in the literal sense: making lines, characters; in the figurative sense: engraving, printing. In the Greek Old Testament, this word often translates the Hebrew term "mikhtab" (writing, letter). The family of "graphô" also includes words like "graphé" (the holy Scripture) and "grammateus" (the scribe).
G1123.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 2:15. Paul uses it to describe how the divine law is "written" in the hearts of non-Jews: even without having received the written Torah, they possess a conscience and knowledge of good engraved within them. This is a key theological argument: Paul shows that all humans have access to moral knowledge, because this law is not merely an external text, but something inscribed deep within their being. The figurative use emphasizes the permanent and unavoidable nature of this inner law.
G1123.portee: This word reminds us that God's law is not just a set of external rules: it is written in the heart of every person, engraved in the conscience. This means that every human being, without exception, possesses knowledge of good and evil, and will be held accountable before God. It is both a source of guilt — we cannot claim ignorance of evil — and a source of hope: God has never left humanity without moral guidance.

sens: the action or art of writing, of tracing characters
a written text, a written passage
a book or written collection
the entirety of the sacred texts of the Old Testament
G1124.detail:
1. The fundamental meaning of the word is the action of writing or tracing characters on a surface. It is the gesture of the hand that forms the letters.

2. Then, the word designates the resulting text: what has been written. A specific passage from the Scriptures is often referred to in the singular, as in Luke 4:21: "this word of Scripture that you have just heard."

3. In the plural, "the Scriptures" refers to the entirety of the sacred texts, the complete collection of inspired books. Jesus says in Matthew 21:42: "Have you never read in the Scriptures?"

4. Sometimes, the word designates Scripture as absolute authority and the word of God. In John 10:35, it is written: "the Scripture cannot be broken," which means that God's written word is indestructible and definitive.
G1124.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "graphō" ("to write"), which carries the image of the act of writing or painting. In Hebrew, it often translates "ketab" ("written") and its derivatives. The Jews of the New Testament period refer to "the Scriptures" as the entirety of what is now called the Old Testament — the Torah, the Prophets, and the Writings. This word carries considerable authority in biblical thought: it is God Himself who has spoken through Scripture.
G1124.emploi: The word "Scripture" or "Scriptures" appears about 50 times in the New Testament, especially in the Gospels and Paul's epistles. Jesus and the apostles constantly use it to quote the Word of God and show how it is fulfilled. In the singular, it designates a specific verse or passage that is quoted or commented on: "what does the Scripture say?" (Romans 4:3). In the plural, "the Scriptures" denotes the entirety of the inspired Word: Jesus tells His disciples in Luke 24:27 that He explained to them what was said about Him "in all the Scriptures." The apostles base their preaching on Scripture: Paul in Acts 17:2 reasons "from the Scriptures" to prove that Jesus was the Messiah. The word carries within it all the authority of God: John 10:35 asserts that "the Scripture cannot be broken."
G1124.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible is much more than an ordinary book: it is Scripture, the written Word of God, indestructible and authoritative. When Jesus and the apostles quote "the Scripture," they teach us to respect it as the voice of God that still speaks to us today. Recognizing Scripture is to submit to God Himself.

sens: To form or trace letters on a surface
To set down words or thoughts in writing, to fix in writing
To record, to document a fact or event
To set down in writing an instruction or order
To adhere to what is written as a word of authority
To communicate in writing to someone
G1125.detail:
1. To form or trace letters on a surface: this is the physical act of writing the letters themselves. In John 8:6-8, Jesus "wrote" on the ground with His finger: it is simply about tracing characters.
2. To set down words or thoughts in writing, to fix in writing: this is translating into written words what was spoken or thought. Luke 1:63 recounts that Zechariah "wrote" the name of John on a tablet: he was documenting an important event through writing.
3. To record, to document a fact or event: to put in writing what has happened, in order to transmit it. John 21:24 states that the disciple "has written these things": he fixes the account of Jesus' life for future generations.
4. To set down in writing an instruction or order: to express a directive in a written and lasting manner. In Mark 10:4-5, the commandment "written" by Moses is mentioned: an order given in writing to be followed.
5. To adhere to what is written as a word of authority: to recognize the holy Scripture as the definitive rule. When it is said "it is written" (for example, Matthew 4:4), the absolute authority of the already established word of God is invoked.
6. To communicate in writing to someone: to send a written message. Romans 15:15: Paul explains that he "writes" to his readers to refresh their memory.
G1125.origine: The verb comes from a very ancient root that originally designated the action of engraving or tracing on a surface. In Hebrew, the verb כתב (katab), which it most often translates in the Septuagint, carries this same idea: to trace characters in a durable manner. The Greek word has been enriched with the meaning of fixing in writing, of putting in written authority. The word family includes compounds like "ἐγγράφω" (to inscribe), "ἐπιγράφω" (to write on, to title) and derived nouns like "γραφή" (Scripture) or "γραμμή" (line).
G1125.emploi: The verb "to write" is one of the most frequent in the New Testament (194 occurrences). It first designates the material act of writing (John 8:6-8, Luke 1:63), then the action of documenting a narrative or teaching (John 21:24, Luke 1:3). A large part of the usages concern the citation of holy Scripture: the formula "it is written" (γέγραπται) introduces the authority of the Old Testament Scriptures as God's definitive word, especially in the words of Jesus or in the letters of Paul (Matthew 4:4, Romans 1:17). Paul also uses the verb to refer to his own letters addressed to the churches (Romans 15:15, Acts 23:25). The tone varies: sometimes it is a practical act, sometimes an act imbued with spiritual authority.
G1125.portee: For the believer, this verb reminds us that the word of God has been fixed in writing to remain and guide: when the Bible says "it is written," it calls for obedience to a stable and authorized word. It also teaches us that what is written in the Gospel is a reliable testimony passed on to future generations, worthy of trust. Writing is the means that God has chosen to preserve and transmit His revelation.

sens: Resembling a tale of an old woman, devoid of meaning or foundation
Futile and of no spiritual value
Contrary to reason and truth
G1126.detail:
1. The word paints the image of a silly story, of the kind that old women tell to amuse children — not a noble or instructive fable, but something hollow and implausible. In 1 Timothy 4:7, Paul exhorts Timothy to reject precisely these "absurd tales," these vain narratives that divert from the truth.
2. It is a word that has no hold on reality, no value of truth: it may entertain or seduce, but it does not nourish faith or knowledge of God.
3. By extension, it is everything that opposes sound doctrine and Christian reason — hollow myths, superstitions, human traditions emptied of spiritual meaning.
G1126.origine: The Greek word comes from a root designating an old woman (graûs) combined with a suffix expressing resemblance (eidos, appearance). The image is that of a word typically "of an old woman" — not out of contempt for women, but because it was an old cliché to designate unfounded tales, superstitions transmitted orally. The word carries within it a judgment: one who accepts such words allows themselves to be deceived by hollow appearances.
G1126.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Timothy 4:7. Paul uses it to warn against erroneous doctrines and human traditions that were beginning to infiltrate the Church, particularly the unfounded ascetic prescriptions mentioned at the beginning of the chapter. It is about protecting believers from any teaching contrary to the truth of Christ, by calling it by its name: a hollow tale, a ridiculous fable.
G1126.portee: This word reminds us that the Christian faith is based on a solid reality — the revelation of God, attested in Scripture — and not on human traditions, superstitious practices, or seductive but empty doctrines. It is an invitation to discern, to listen to what is true and useful, and to courageously reject what leads away from Christ and the Gospel.

sens: Stay awake, do not sleep
Guard, watch over, be a sentinel
Be vigilant, attentive, on guard
Be spiritually alert to danger or the return of Christ
G1127.detail:
1. Stay awake, do not sleep: this is the simplest meaning, that of the body remaining conscious. Jesus asks his disciples: "stay here, and watch with me" (Matthew 26:38), asking them to stay awake by his side while he prays.
2. Guard, watch over, be a sentinel: this is to watch like a doorkeeper who oversees a house (Mark 13:34), or like a thief who is ready to enter; this meaning implies active attention, responsibility.
3. Be vigilant, attentive, on guard: one watches to avoid being caught off guard or to be ready to act. The one who watches will find the master upon his arrival "watching," that is, ready and faithful (Luke 12:37).
4. Be spiritually vigilant in the face of danger or the return of Christ: "Watch, for you do not know what day your Lord will come" (Matthew 24:42); Paul exhorts: "Watch, stand firm in the faith" (1 Corinthians 16:13); the Christian must watch against the attacks of the evil one like a vigilant soldier.
G1127.origine: The word comes from the Greek that expresses the state of being awake (it is built on the verb "to wake up"). In Hebrew from the Old Testament, this word often translates a verb meaning "to be alert, to be attentive." Watching is therefore the state opposite to sleep, but beyond simple physical sleep: it is the attitude of one who is conscious and ready.
G1127.emploi: The verb appears 23 times in the New Testament, mostly in Matthew (5 times), Mark (6 times), and in the Pauline epistles. In the Gospels, "watch" primarily describes the physical action of staying awake beside Jesus (Matthew 26:38, Mark 14:34) or the concrete task of a vigilant servant (Mark 13:34, Luke 12:37). But very quickly the meaning becomes spiritual and eschatological: "Watch, for you do not know what day your Lord will come" (Matthew 24:42, 25:13). In Paul and Peter, watching becomes the permanent attitude of the believer in the face of temptations and judgment: "Watch at all times" (Colossians 4:2), "Your adversary, the devil, prowls around like a roaring lion; be sober-minded, watch" (1 Peter 5:8).
G1127.portee: This word calls the Christian to a constant vigilance: not anxiety, but conscious attention to the return of Christ and the spiritual dangers that threaten his faith. To watch means to be active in one's relationship with God, attentive to His Word, ready to obey. It is also a promise: the vigilant believer will be found faithful and will receive a reward from the Lord.

sens: Properly, to exercise naked, like Greek athletes in the palestra
Train the body or mind through regular practice
Accustom someone to something through repeated use
Make skilled or capable through experience
G1128.detail:
1. The word comes from the Greek image of the athlete who trains naked in the palestra: "γυμνάζω" has its root in "γυμνός" (naked). This is the visible etymology of the French word "gymnase."

2. More broadly, "exercise" means to train the body or mind through repetition: in Hebrews 5:14, the judgment of mature individuals is "exercised by use to discern" good from evil, like a muscle that is strengthened.

3. It is also to gradually accustom: those who have been "exercised" by discipline in Hebrews 12:11 have learned through suffering, they have become accustomed to receiving correction. Repeated experience shapes character.

4. Among the false teachers in 2 Peter 2:14, the heart is "exercised in greed": they have become skilled in sin, practicing it continuously until they have mastered it.
G1128.origine: The verb "γυμνάζω" comes from the Greek "γυμνός" (gymná, "naked"), the adjective that describes the state of nudity of athletes training. This naked training was a characteristic practice of ancient Greek culture. The corresponding Hebrew word is often "שׁמר" (shamar, "to keep") or "עִמַּל" (ammal, "to work with toil"), but "γυμνάζω" rather conveys the idea of intentional and regular practice to develop a skill or character trait.
G1128.emploi: The verb appears four times in the New Testament, all uses being figurative: never for physical sport, always for spiritual or moral training. In 1 Timothy 4:7, Paul exhorts to reject "profane myths" — here, the Greek text says "exercise yourself for godliness" (γυμνάζε σεαυτόν), to emphasize the deliberate training towards virtue. In Hebrews 5:14, it is moral judgment that must be exercised by use. In Hebrews 12:11, discipline exercises the one who endures it, forming him to righteousness. In 2 Peter 2:14, the false teachers have exercised their hearts in covetousness: they have hardened themselves in vice.
G1128.portee: This word reminds the Christian that faith and virtue are not acquired through sudden illumination, but through regular training, like an athlete who exercises. The disciple must exercise his judgment (Hebrews 5:14), accept the exercise of discipline (Hebrews 12:11), and guard against exercising his heart in sin (2 Peter 2:14). It is an invitation to progressive spiritual discipline and vigilance.

sens: Regular and repeated practice to develop an ability or skill
Training of the body through physical activity
G1129.detail:
1. Regular and repeated practice to develop an ability or skill: this is the general idea of training, whether mental or physical. The word evokes the effort that one repeats to progress and improve.
2. Training of the body through physical activity: in particular, it is the muscular work, the bodily effort that one repeats. In 1 Timothy 4:8, Paul distinguishes this bodily "exercise" from spiritual piety, recognizing that the body needs to be trained, but that the formation of the soul has a much deeper and lasting value.
G1129.origine: The word comes from the verb "γυμνάζω" (gymnazô), which means "to train" or "to exercise," itself derived from "γυμνός" (gymnós, "naked"). Originally, in ancient Greece, athletes trained naked in the gymnasium, hence the name of this training. The word has retained the idea of intensive and regular training, whether done as an athlete or in a broader sense.
G1129.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Timothy 4:8. Paul uses it to speak of bodily exercise, which he recognizes as useful, but to which he opposes spiritual piety, which is much more useful. The pastoral context shows that he is addressing a young pastor who must take care of his body, but without confusing this physical discipline with true spiritual formation, which alone prepares for eternal life.
G1129.portee: This verse reminds us that a healthy balance is welcome: taking care of one's body through regular activity has value. But Paul also invites us to discern priorities: the formation of our heart, our walk with God, our growth in piety has infinitely greater value, as it prepares us not only for this life but for eternal life. It is a word of wisdom against the overvaluation of the body and fitness in our culture.

sens: to be without clothing
to be poorly dressed
to lack the necessities
G1130.detail:
1. To be naked literally means to have no clothing on oneself — a state of complete physical destitution. In 1 Corinthians 4:11, Paul says, "we suffer hunger, thirst, nakedness": he refers to a situation of absolute lack.
2. To be poorly dressed or "scantily clad" describes one who has only rags, torn or worn-out clothing — a partial nakedness that exposes poverty. It is the state of one who cannot cover themselves decently.
3. To lack the necessities is the figurative sense: to be naked means to be devoid not only of clothing but of everything that protects, warms, and gives dignity. It is one of the three great deprivations listed by Paul alongside hunger and thirst.
G1130.origine: The Greek γυμνός (gymnos) means "naked"; the verb γυμνητεύω is derived from it with the suffix -ευω which forms action verbs. The verb literally means "to be in a naked state," "to have nakedness." The basic image is that of a body without protection, without covering — a nakedness that is both physical and social, for in antiquity a naked man is a man without dignity, without resources.
G1130.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament: 1 Corinthians 4:11, where Paul lists the sufferings of the apostles. It is juxtaposed with "hunger" and "thirst" — three elemental lacks that summarize extreme poverty. Paul is not speaking of moral or spiritual nakedness, but of concrete material misery: the apostles lacked food and clothing. Elsewhere, the adjective "naked" (γυμνοί) appears in James 2:15 to describe a destitute person; the biblical context always associates this nakedness with lack, distress, and vulnerability.
G1130.portee: This word reminds the reader that a life of authentic Christian service may require renouncing all material comfort. Paul cites it not to evoke pity, but to affirm that the Gospel is worth much more than bodily security. It also unmasks complacency: if the apostles experienced nakedness and hunger, how can a Christian ignore one who is shivering and hungry? (James 2:15).

sens: Devoid of clothing, without garment on the body
Poorly or simply dressed
Exposed, laid bare without protection
Deprived of the physical body, spiritually alone
G1131.detail:
1. In the strict sense, to be naked means to have no clothing on oneself: one thinks of the young man who flees without anything in Mark 14:52 ("he left his garment and fled away naked"), or the possessed men who find themselves naked and wounded after their encounter with demons in Acts 19:16. It is the complete absence of clothing.
2. Sometimes, to be naked describes a condition of poverty, of material insufficiency: this is the case of the brother or sister "naked and lacking daily food" in James 2:15, where the word designates one who has nothing to cover themselves or to eat.
3. Figuratively, to be naked means to be exposed, laid bare without defense or secret: Hebrews 4:13 says that "all things are naked and open to the eyes of Him to whom we must give account," an image of absolute transparency before God.
4. For the soul or spirit, to be naked means to be detached from the physical body, as in 2 Corinthians 5:3 where Paul fears being found "naked" at the moment of leaving this world.
G1131.origine: The Greek word "gymnos" comes from a root that evokes the absence of covering. In Hebrew, the same concept is found with the word "arôm" (עָרוֹם), which notably designates the naked body, and this word has given rise to other Hebrew words related to nakedness or the corpse. The Greek "gymnos" is also the ancestor of our French word "gymnase," a place where athletes in antiquity trained naked.
G1131.emploi: This word appears 15 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and the epistles. Matthew 25 uses it six times in Jesus' discourse on the final judgment: clothing the hungry or the naked becomes the criterion for salvation. Mark 14:51-52 recounts the flight of the naked young man during Jesus' arrest. Paul in 2 Corinthians 5:3 uses it to explore the state of the soul without a body. In Revelation, the word takes on a spiritual significance: to be naked is to be spiritually poor and miserable (Revelation 3:17). The meaning thus nuances from the physical (absence of clothing) to the social (poverty) to the spiritual (exposure before God, or spiritual poverty).
G1131.portee: For the Christian, this word invites one to look at the poor and abandoned with the eyes of Jesus. Clothing the naked is not a mere surface charitable act: it is recognizing Christ in the destitute. It also calls for spiritual honesty: nothing is hidden from God, and the nakedness of our condition before Him should lead us to sincerity and humility. Finally, for one who knows themselves to be spiritually poor, this word offers a salutary provocation: true wealth is not in clothing or appearances, but in the presence of God.

sens: Absence of clothing, state of the body being naked
Material destitution, lack of what is necessary
Shame, dishonor attached to being uncovered or without resources
Spiritual vulnerability, absence of divine protection
G1132.detail:
1. The primary and concrete sense: to be without clothing, to have the body naked. Paul speaks of it as a physical trial he experienced, alongside hunger and cold (2 Corinthians 11:27) — it is a brutal and humiliating destitution.
2. By extension, nakedness designates material destitution, absolute lack: one who has neither clothing nor covering to protect against the cold is without resources. It is one of the tribulations that Paul lists in Romans 8:35, where it appears among the evils that could separate us from God.
3. Nakedness carries a moral weight: it is a shame, a shameful exposure. In Revelation 3:18, the church of Laodicea is threatened with seeing "the shame of its nakedness" appear — in other words, its spiritual unworthiness revealed to all.
4. Spiritually, it is the absence of spiritual clothing, the state of one who has not received the righteousness of Christ, who remains vulnerable and dishonored before God. Revelation invites one to buy "white garments" so as not to remain naked — an image of justification.
G1132.origine: The Greek word comes from the adjective "gymnos" (naked). It appears in the Greek translation of the Old Testament to render the Hebrew "érom" (naked, bare). The root evokes the idea of being exposed, without protection or covering — literally removing clothing, but also, figuratively, being devoid of everything. The family of the Greek word includes "gymnase" (place of exercise where one was partially naked) and "gymnastique" (to exercise).
G1132.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, always in Paul and in Revelation, never in the Gospels. It is first used in the physical and concrete sense: Paul enumerates what he endured as an apostle — nakedness is alongside hunger, cold, and persecution (Romans 8:35 and 2 Corinthians 11:27), which shows that it is a true deprivation, a trial of destitution. It then takes on a spiritual and moral hue in Revelation, where nakedness symbolizes the absence of righteousness, spiritual unworthiness: it is a "shame" from which the church must clothe itself in white garments to escape.
