In all cases, the word designates a state of deprivation and vulnerability — physical, social, or spiritual.
G1132.portee: For a Christian, this word reminds us of two things. First, that the apostles experienced extreme material destitution out of faithfulness to Christ, and that nothing we suffer physically can separate us from His love (Romans 8:35). Secondly, and more profoundly, that our spiritual nakedness — our lack of personal righteousness — is covered by the "white garments" of the risen Christ. Nakedness is shame and vulnerability; it is redeemed only by His grace.

sens: despised or weak-willed woman
easily deceived or manipulated person
mind without solid judgment
G1133.detail:
1. The word designates a woman with a nuance of contempt or condescension — not an ordinary woman, but one considered insignificant or lacking moral strength. In 2 Timothy 3:6, Paul speaks of women "weighed down by sins and led by various desires" that false teachers seek to seduce: these are not all women, but those deemed easy to deceive.
2. The image is that of a person without inner strength, lacking the ability to discern truth from falsehood, and therefore vulnerable to manipulation. These women are "loaded down with sins" and "swayed by passions" (2 Timothy 3:6), which makes them even more exposed to seducers.
G1133.origine: The word is formed from the diminutive "-arion" added to "guné" (γυνή), which means woman. This suffix, instead of creating an affectionate or tender form (like "little woman"), expresses here contempt or devaluation: it refers to a woman who is diminished, weak, or insignificant. It is a pejorative formation, typical of how one might speak disdainfully of a person.
G1133.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Timothy 3:6. Paul uses it in a passage where he describes ungodly men infiltrating Christian communities to destroy them from within: these seducers particularly target women of weak temperament — not women in general, but those whose moral judgment is not firmly established or who are prey to passions. The choice of the pejorative diminutive reinforces the criticism: Paul points out not only the weakness of these women but also the ignominy of those who exploit them.
G1133.portee: This word reminds us that moral weakness — lack of discernment, agitation of passions, absence of solid foundation — renders one vulnerable to deception and manipulation. It invites everyone, man or woman, to strengthen their faith, cultivate judgment, and resist temptations. It is a call to spiritual vigilance and maturity in Christ.

sens: Belonging to the female sex, to women
Characteristic of the nature and traits of women
Expressing physical fragility or the inferior condition recognized for women in society
G1134.detail:
1. The word designates what belongs to or relates to women, in contrast to men — it is the adjective "feminine" in its simplest sense. In 1 Peter 3:7, Peter refers to wives as "the weaker sex" literally saying "the weaker vessel."
2. It characterizes what is inherent to women in their very nature: their distinctive traits, their physical condition. The apostle acknowledges that women possess a constitution that is physically less robust than that of men.
3. In the context of 1 Peter 3:7, the word emphasizes the relative fragility of women and, by extension, a social position that was considered subordinate or vulnerable at the time — which underpins the exhortation for husbands to honor and treat them with respect.
G1134.origine: The word comes from the Greek gunè (woman) and carries the suffix -eios which forms adjectives. It literally designates "that which is of the woman" or "that which belongs to the woman." It is a simple and transparent derivative of the root designating the female sex. The corresponding Hebrew word in the Septuagint is most often ishshah (woman, wife).
G1134.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 3:7. Peter uses it in an exhortation addressed to husbands: he invites them to live wisely with their wives, recognizing that the female sex is physically weaker. This mention serves to justify a respectful and honorable treatment: precisely because women are more fragile, husbands must honor them as co-heirs of the grace of eternal life. The apostle does not rely on weakness to justify contempt, but rather to demand special care.
G1134.portee: This passage, the only mention of this word in the Bible, invites us to look beyond a physical observation to recognize the complete dignity of the wife in God's eyes. The Christian husband is called to combine two realities: the acknowledgment of a difference in physical constitution and the affirmation that the woman is a co-heir of divine grace. It is a call to honor and protect the one received as a companion and partner before God.

sens: Person of the female sex, adult or young girl
Wife, woman married to a man
Female deacon or servant of the Church
G1135G.detail:
1. The word simply designates a woman, married or unmarried, in her general human dimension. It is the common term for speaking of a person of the female sex (Matthew 5:28: "whoever looks at a woman to lust after her"; Mark 14:3: "a woman came… holding an alabaster jar"). The vocative "Woman" (John 2:4, 4:21) does not express contempt but rather respect and tenderness.
2. The word also designates a woman in her marital relationship, the wife. She is "married to a man" (Romans 7:2) or has the status of a wife in the household (Matthew 1:20). The Bible speaks of "having a wife" or "taking a wife" to express marriage.
3. Rarely, the word can also refer to a woman who holds a position in the Church, notably a deacon (1 Timothy 3:11), that is, a woman recognized for her service in the Christian community.
G1135G.origine: The Greek word gunē comes from an ancient root that expresses the idea of "she who gives birth" or "she who is born." It corresponds to the Hebrew word ishshah (אִשָּׁה) from the Old Testament, which has the same root as ish ("man"), emphasizing that the woman is the companion of man. In Greek, this word is the direct equivalent of the Hebrew term in the ancient translations of the Old Testament.
G1135G.emploi: This word appears more than 116 times in the New Testament, particularly in the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John) and in Acts. It describes both women who appear in a narrative (the Samaritan woman in John 4, the adulterous woman in John 8:3) and central figures (Elizabeth, Mary). The uses show respect towards women: they are active in faith (Acts 5:14: "more and more believers were added to the Lord, both men and women"), they seek Jesus for healing (Mark 5:25-34), they are witnesses of the Resurrection (Luke 24:22). The word can also qualify the wife (Romans 7:2) or refer to community imagery (Ephesians 5, where the Church is the bride).
G1135G.portee: This word invites us to see how the Bible elevates the dignity of women. They are not an inferior category, but a full person, created in the image of God. The Gospels show Jesus speaking to women with respect (John 4:7-28, where he speaks to a Samaritan woman alone at the well), healing sick women, and entrusting women with the first message of the Resurrection. For the Christian, this calls to honor women as sisters and to recognize their essentially equal place in the body of Christ.

sens: A person of the female sex, married or single
The wife of a man, united to him by marriage
A female deacon or minister in the assembly
G1135H.detail:
1. The word simply designates a person of the female sex, without restriction of marital status. In Luke 1:18, Zechariah speaks of his "wife" who is elderly, which evokes a whole life lived together. The word is also used in situations unrelated to marriage, to refer to a woman in the crowd or as a witness (Matthew 27:19, where a woman, the governor's wife, intervenes in the trial of Jesus).
2. The most common meaning is that of a wife bound to her husband by the marriage covenant. "Joseph took his wife with him" (Matthew 1:20 and 1:24) or "he left his wife to his brother" (Matthew 22:25) show this marital bond. The Apostle Paul extensively develops this relationship: "the husband must give his wife her conjugal rights" (1 Corinthians 7:3).
3. In 1 Timothy 3:11, there is mention of women (probably deaconesses) who assist in the service of the assembly, mentioned alongside the deacons, suggesting an official role of minister or servant in the church.
G1135H.origine: The Greek word γυνή comes from an ancient root designating woman and femininity. In the Septuagint, it regularly translates the Hebrew word אִשָּׁה (isha), which means both "woman" and "wife." This family of words also includes the adjective γυναικεῖος (gynaikeios, feminine) and compounds like ἀνδρόγυνος. The Hebrew word it translates carries the idea of a companion, one who shares the life of a man.
G1135H.emploi: The word γυνή appears about 83 times in the New Testament, notably in the Gospels and Pauline epistles. It is primarily used to designate a woman in everyday life (a widow, a sinner, a sick person), and secondly, and very frequently, to speak of the wife in the context of marriage. Paul outlines her role in 1 Corinthians 7 (conjugal duty, widowhood, remarriage) and in Ephesians 5 (the loving relationship between spouses as an image of Christ and the Church). The word is also used vocatively (addressing a woman) in Matthew 15:28 and John 2:4, where it carries no severity but rather marks respect and tenderness.
G1135H.portee: This word reminds us of the central place of women in God's plan: they are not objects but whole persons, worthy of respect and love. Paul's teachings on marriage show that the union of man and woman reflects the mystery of Christ and the Church, thus elevating marriage to the status of a spiritual image. For the Christian, understanding this term invites recognition of the dignity of every woman and living marital relationships as a form of mutual giving.

sens: Eschatological character or power associated with Magog
G1136.detail: Gog is mentioned in Revelation 20:8 alongside Magog as an enemy power that Satan raises at the end of times to attack the nations. This name designates either a leader, a kingdom, or a hostile force that represents the final opposition to the people of God before the final judgment.
G1136.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew גּוֹג (Gog). In the Greek Old Testament, this name evokes the prophecy of Ezekiel (chapters 38-39) which speaks of a leader from the land of Magog who will threaten Israel. The New Testament takes up this image of Gog and Magog to symbolize the powers of evil at the end of history.
G1136.emploi: Gog appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 20:8. John mentions him at the time of the last rebellion against God, after the millennial reign of Christ. Gog and Magog form a pair: Magog seems to be the place or the people, while Gog could be the leader or the power. Together, they symbolize Satan's last attempt to draw the nations against the people of God, and this rebellion will be crushed by divine judgment.
G1136.portee: For the Christian, Gog and Magog remind us that opposition to God does not disappear until the last day, and that even after a long period of peace, evil will seek to resurface. This encourages the believer to remain vigilant and to place their trust in the promised final victory of Christ, which alone will ultimately defeat all rebellion.

sens: Corner of a street or intersection
Angle of a building, corner of a structure
Cornerstone, chief stone of a construction
Remote, hidden, secret place
G1137.detail:
1. The corner of a street or intersection, a place where several paths meet: hypocrites loved to pray "on the corners of the streets" (Matthew 6:5) to be seen, where many people passed.
2. The angle or corner of a building, the point where two walls meet: this is how the Bible speaks of the "cornerstone," the main stone that unites and supports the entire structure of the building (Matthew 21:42).
3. The cornerstone in a figurative sense: the one rejected by the builders but becomes the most important, the essential — an image of the Messiah in the Old Testament taken up by Jesus and the apostles (Acts 4:11).
4. A remote, hidden place, away from sight: Paul says that the Gospel was not spread "in secret" (Acts 26:26), but openly.
G1137.origine: The Greek word comes from the root γόνυ (gonu, "knee"), the basic image being that of two lines or surfaces meeting and bending, like the two bones of the knee that articulate. In Hebrew, the word פִּנָּה (pinnah) has the same meaning: a corner, an angle, a junction place. This family of words expresses the idea of curvature and meeting.
G1137.emploi: The word appears 9 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels and Acts. Matthew, Mark, and Luke use it to designate the "corner of the streets" where hypocrites prayed (Matthew 6:5) and to quote Psalm 118:22 about the "cornerstone" that was rejected and then became the chief (Matthew 21:42, Mark 12:10, Luke 20:17). Acts also takes up this same citation (Acts 4:11) and applies it to the risen Jesus Christ. The word can also mean a hidden or secret place (Acts 26:26). In Revelation 7:1 and 20:8, the "four corners of the earth" refer to the four corners of the world, that is, the entirety of creation. Peter's Epistle also cites the Psalm speaking of the "cornerstone" (1 Peter 2:7).
G1137.portee: Understanding this word helps the reader grasp one of the most beautiful messianic prophecies in the Bible: that of the "cornerstone." Rejected, despised, this stone becomes the main element, the support of the entire edifice — a promise that God transforms human refusals into the fulfillment of His will. It is the assurance that even what seems broken or rejected in the believer's life can become essential in God's plan.

sens: King of Israel, anointed by the prophet Samuel to succeed Saul.
Ancestor of Jesus according to the messianic genealogy.
Type figure of the Messiah, foreshadowing the kingship and wisdom of Christ.
The traditional author of the Psalms, whose prophetic words announce Christ.
In the expressions 'son of David' and 'house of David': the Messiah coming from the Davidic royal lineage, and the messianic dynasty.
G1138.detail:
1. David is the king of Israel anointed by the prophet Samuel after Saul's rejection. He becomes the prototype of the true king in biblical tradition and reigns from Jerusalem, establishing a kingdom that lasts for several centuries.

2. David is the direct ancestor of Jesus according to the genealogical lineage that Matthew places at the beginning of his Gospel (Matthew 1:1). This ancestry is crucial: Jesus is announced as 'Son of David' from his conception (Luke 1:27).

3. David foreshadows the Messiah in his kingship, his victory over enemies, and his position seated at the right hand of God. Jesus himself cites David to show that the Messiah is more than just a descendant: he is the Lord of David (Matthew 22:42-45).

4. David is recognized as the author of the Psalms. In Hebrews 4:7, the text says 'in David', which means 'in the Psalter'. David's words prophetically announce Christ: thus Psalm 110 (quoted in Acts 2:25-35) reveals the Resurrection and exaltation of the Messiah.

5. The titles 'son of David' and 'house of David' become designations of the awaited Messiah. The blind men in Jericho cry 'Son of David' in recognizing Jesus (Mark 10:47); the key of David and the throne of David (Revelation 3:7; Luke 1:32) symbolize absolute messianic authority.
G1138.origine: The Hebrew name דָּוִד (Dawid) likely means 'beloved'. In late Jewish tradition, David embodies the model of the just king and servant of God. The Psalms attributed to David have been read by the early Christian generations as prophetic announcements of Christ: this messianic reinterpretation, attested in rabbinic texts and pseudepigrapha (Psalms of Solomon), explains why the New Testament constantly cites David to prove that Jesus is the Messiah.
G1138.emploi: David appears 54 times in the New Testament, especially in the first three Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke) and in Acts. He is mentioned in the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:1-17), in the prophetic announcements concerning the birth of the Messiah (Luke 1:69), and in Jesus' debates with the Pharisees (Matthew 22:41-45). Acts uses David to prove to Israel that Jesus is the promised Messiah: Peter cites the Psalms of David (Acts 2:25; 4:25). Revelation uses Davidic titles ('root of David', Revelation 5:5; 'key of David', Revelation 3:7) to designate Jesus as heir to the throne and true king. David is also the model of faith cited in Hebrews 11:32.
G1138.portee: David reminds the reader that the Messiah did not appear out of nowhere, but is part of an Israelite history, a genealogy, a promise. Knowing David helps to understand that Jesus fulfills the hopes of God's people. The titles 'son of David' and the symbols of the Davidic throne show that Jesus truly reigns, not as an earthly king, but as an eternal king whose Father has established a kingdom without end (Luke 1:32-33).

sens: To be possessed by a demon, under its influence
To be tormented or ill due to a demon
To experience demonic control over body and mind
G1139.detail:
1. The word describes the state of someone who is possessed by a demon (or demons), meaning that an evil spirit has taken possession of them and controls them. In Matthew 8:28, the two demoniacs are so violently controlled that no one can pass near them; in Mark 5:15, after Jesus frees them, the same man is 'in his right mind' — which shows that before, he had lost control of himself.
2. Demonic possession manifests through various sufferings: mutism (Matthew 9:32), madness or disordered behavior (Mark 5:15), sometimes paralysis or blindness (Matthew 12:22). The Canaanite woman says of her daughter that she is 'cruelly tormented by a demon' (Matthew 15:22) — torment is the sign of hostile presence.
3. Jesus encounters these individuals and frees them by his authority: he commands the demon to come out, and the man returns to himself. This is an act of power and compassion that shows Jesus' victory over the demonic world.
G1139.origine: The word comes from δαίμων (daimôn, 'demon') and the suffix -ζομαι (-zomai), which forms a passive or middle verb: literally 'to be made demonic' or 'to be acted upon by a demon'. In the Hebrew and Aramaic of the Old Testament, texts speak more of 'evil spirits' or possession by evil; the Greek word 'demon' takes up this reality but with a new sharpness in the New Testament: it refers to spiritual beings hostile to God and humans.
G1139.emploi: This verb appears 13 times in the New Testament, almost always in the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John) and always in participial form: one speaks of 'the one who is demonic' or 'a demoniac'. Matthew uses it most often, particularly in healing narratives: the mute demoniac (9:32), the Canaanite woman’s daughter (15:22), the demoniacs of Gadara (8:28). Mark and Luke report similar cases. In Matthew 4:24, 'demoniacs' is listed among other ailments brought to Jesus — which shows that possession was considered a serious illness, distinct from mere physical illness. After liberation, the word also marks the change: in Mark 5:18, the one who 'had been demonic' asks to follow Jesus.
G1139.portee: The Bible shows that demonic possession is a serious spiritual reality, not a superstition or purely psychological illness. But it also affirms that Jesus has absolute authority over demons: he casts them out with a single word. This reassures the Christian who recognizes the existence of spiritual warfare but knows that Jesus' power is greater than that of evil. Jesus' encounters with demoniacs also show his compassion: he comes to free the captives, restore their dignity and their freedom.

sens: Evil spiritual being that possesses and torments humans
Unclean spirit that seizes a person and controls them
Power of evil opposed to God and His kingdom
False deity worshiped by idolatrous peoples
In classical Greek usage: divine power or any supernatural being
G1140.detail:
1. A demon is an evil spiritual being that enters a person and possesses them, making them sick, insane, or tormented. The man possessed by a legion of demons (Luke 8:30) can no longer control himself; the woman possessed by an unclean spirit for eighteen years is bent over and cannot straighten up (Luke 13:32). Jesus frees these possessed individuals by casting out the demons from them.
2. The demon is an unclean spirit, an evil and intelligent power that knows Jesus (Mark 1:34) and refuses to obey His disciples (Luke 9:49). The Twelve receive the authority to cast out demons in the name of Jesus (Matthew 10:8).
3. The demons serve the prince of demons, Beelzebul, who organizes evil against the kingdom of God (Matthew 12:24). To fight demons is to fight the reign of evil itself; when Jesus casts them out, the kingdom of God arrives (Matthew 12:28).
4. In the Old Testament interpreted by the Greeks, the word δαιμόνιον translates the false gods of idolaters: when Israel offers sacrifices, it is actually worshiping demons (1 Corinthians 10:20).
5. In classical Greek, the word could simply refer to a deity, a neutral supernatural power, but the New Testament applies it exclusively to evil spirits.
G1140.origine: The word comes from the adjective δαιμόνιος ("divine," "sacred") itself formed from δαίμων (demon, spirit, supernatural power). In classical Greek, a δαίμων was a kind of spirit or power intermediate between gods and humans. The New Testament takes this word to designate the evil powers that torment humans — what the Greek translation of the Old Testament calls the false gods and idols worshiped by the nations. For biblical authors, the deities of pagan peoples are nothing but demons.
G1140.emploi: The word appears 55 times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in the Gospels and in the epistles. The first three Gospels frequently report that Jesus casts out demons as a sign of judgment on the powers of evil: over thirty passages. Mark and Luke particularly emphasize the possessed individuals freed by Jesus (Luke 8:2, Mark 5:15). The disciples receive the power to cast out demons (Matthew 10:8, Luke 9:1). In John and the epistles, the word appears less often, but always to describe the opposition of evil to God: demons know that there is one God (James 2:19), and false teachings are "doctrines of demons" (1 Timothy 4:1). Revelation shows demons gathered for the final battle (Revelation 16:14).
G1140.portee: The word demon reminds the Christian that evil is not merely an absence of good, but a personal, intelligent, and organized reality that seeks to destroy humanity. But the Bible clearly affirms that Jesus has defeated the demons and that authority over them belongs to His disciples: the Christian is not left defenseless against these powers. Recognizing the existence of demons is to take spiritual warfare seriously and to seek in Jesus protection and deliverance.

sens: That which comes from demons or resembles them
That which manifests a wicked opposition to God's plan
That which pertains to worldly and carnal wisdom, not from God
G1141.detail: 1. The word literally describes what is of the nature of demons, what comes from them or resembles them — something distinctly demonic. 2. In James 3:15, it qualifies a certain "wisdom" that is not from above (that of God), but comes from the earth, from the carnal heart, from human selfishness: it is therefore diabolical, contrary to God. The contrast is clear: heavenly and pure wisdom on one side, earthly and diabolical wisdom on the other. This kind of wisdom leads people to quarrel, to be jealous, to boast, to lie — all that destroys the Christian community. The word is used only once in the New Testament, which shows that James uses very strong language to describe the fruits of pride and covetousness.
G1141.origine: The word comes from δαιμόνιον (demon, evil spirit) and the suffix -ώδης which means "similar to, having the aspect of." Literally: "having the aspect of a demon." This formation reminds us that demons are indeed real in biblical thought; to qualify something as diabolical is to place it on the side of the powers opposing God. In Hebrew, there are similar terms to speak of what is wicked, evil, opposed to God.
G1141.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in James 3:15. James uses it to stigmatize a "wisdom" that arises from envy, selfishness, and ambition: it is earthly (from the realm of sinful world), carnal (from the unrenewed human nature), and diabolical (inspired by evil powers, contrary to God). James opposes this wisdom to that which comes "from above," wise, peaceful, and gentle. This diabolical wisdom leads to divisions, quarrels, and all the fruits of sin in the Christian assembly. The choice of this very strong word shows the urgency and gravity of the message: to follow such wisdom is to side with rebellion against God.
G1141.portee: For the Christian reader, this word invites discernment regarding the sources of their wisdom and thoughts. Are we seeking the wisdom that comes from above, from God — humble, gentle, peaceable — or that which arises from pride, envy, ambition? James warns us that thoughts, even if they seem wise, can be inspired by lies and rebellion. Knowing this word helps to identify in ourselves and around us what truly comes from God and what is far from Him.

sens: Evil spirit, invisible creature subject to Satan
Hostile power against God and man, capable of possessing a person
G1142.detail:
1. The word "demon" designates a malevolent spiritual creature, an invisible being that opposes God and His kingdom. Unlike angels, who serve God, demons are rebellious spirits that seek to harm humans. In the two passages where it appears, the demons recognize Jesus' superior authority by asking Him where to go after their expulsion.
2. Demons have the ability to inhabit a person's body and dominate them. In Matthew 8:31 and Mark 5:12, the demons that possessed a man beg Jesus, instead of being annihilated, to send them into a herd of pigs: they seek another refuge, another creature to inhabit. This image shows that demons have real power, but always limited and subject to that of Jesus.
G1142.origine: The Greek word "daimōn" comes from an ancient root that first designates a spirit or a deity. In classical Greek, it could have a more neutral meaning, but in the New Testament, it always takes on a distinctly hostile and evil meaning. The term is closely related to "daimonion" (demonium), a more common diminutive form that appears in the same contexts. In Isaiah 65:11, the Hebrew word "gad" (minor divine creature or spirit) is translated by this term, showing how biblical thought views spirits contrary to the Lord.
G1142.emploi: The word "demon" is very rare in its simple form "daimōn": it appears only twice, both in parallel accounts in Matthew and Mark regarding the demoniac of Gadara. In these two verses (Matthew 8:31 and Mark 5:12), Jesus casts out an evil spirit, and several demons collectively beg Jesus to send them into the nearby herd of pigs. The context shows that the demons recognize Jesus as superior, that they fear the abyss (hell), and that they are subject to His absolute authority. These two usages reveal the biblical reality of possession and the liberating power of Jesus.
G1142.portee: These two passages show that spiritual warfare is real: demons truly exist and seek to possess and destroy. But Jesus has total authority over them; He needs only a word to cast them out. The demon must obey Christ. For the believer, this guarantees that no one can be left to these hostile powers without recourse: the power of Jesus is limitless and available to deliver.

sens: To make a wound with the teeth
To attack someone with malice
To cause harm, destroy a community
G1143.detail:
1. To bite means to sink the teeth into something or someone, to make a wound. It is the literal and physical action of an animal defending itself or attacking.
2. To bite is also said of someone who attacks another with wickedness and hostility, as if to injure or dominate. It is an image of aggression.
3. Biting, used figuratively in Galatians 5:15, describes how Christians can destroy one another: "If you bite and devour one another," meaning they harm each other through malice, quarrels, and lack of charity, until they ruin the entire community.
G1143.origine: The verb δάκνω (daknō) comes from an Indo-European root that imitates the act of biting. In Hebrew, the word נשׁךְ (nashak) has the same meaning: to make a wound with the teeth, or, figuratively, to harm someone. The Greek word is used to translate this Hebrew verb in several passages of the Greek Old Testament. The image is universal: a bite is an attack, a way to dominate or destroy.
G1143.emploi: The verb to bite appears only once in the New Testament, in Galatians 5:15, where Paul uses it figuratively. He urges the Galatians to stop fighting one another — to "bite" each other. This violent language shows how division and malice destroy a community and echoes the Old Testament, where biting is often the image of betrayal, rebellion, or divine judgment (for example, Genesis 49:17, where the serpent bites the heel of the rider). Paul borrows this image to warn that aggressive behavior among Christians leads to self-destruction.
G1143.portee: This word reminds every believer that division, jealousy, and quarrels among brothers do much more harm than one might think: they can destroy the testimony and unity of the Church. To bite one's brother is to submit to the flesh rather than to the Spirit, and to forget the love that should reign among the disciples of Jesus.

sens: A drop of water that flows from the eye
Tears, emotional expression
A sign of pain, repentance, or compassion
Expression of the depth of love
Overcome or comforted suffering
G1144.detail:
1. A tear is primarily the drop of water that flows from the eye when one cries. It is the physical phenomenon: it wets the feet of Jesus (Luke 7:38), flows abundantly (Acts 20:31 specifies that Paul weeps night and day).
2. It expresses deep emotion: pain, repentance, or affection. The sinful woman manifests through her tears humility and gratitude towards Jesus (Luke 7:44), while Paul teaches with tears those he loves like a pastor (Acts 20:19).
3. The tear becomes the visible symbol of inner distress or intercession. Jesus himself prays "with tears" (Hebrews 5:7), showing the intensity of his struggle.
4. It can also convey extreme love or pastoral concern: Paul writes to the Corinthians "with many tears" to tenderly warn them (2 Corinthians 2:4).
5. Finally, in the vision of Revelation, tears are wiped from every face: God himself "will wipe away every tear from their eyes" (Revelation 21:4), a promise of ultimate comfort.
G1144.origine: The Greek word δάκρυον comes from an ancient root that denotes weeping and is found in many Indo-European languages. It regularly translates the Hebrew דִּמְעָה (dimâ) in the Greek Old Testament. The word expresses one of the most universal manifestations of human emotion, and its poetic form δάκρυ shows that it has always carried a strong emotional charge.
G1144.emploi: The word appears about 11 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Paul's epistles. In Luke 7, the tears of the sinful woman mark her transformation and love for the Savior. Paul uses the word to describe his own pastoral ministry: he weeps while preaching (Acts 20:19, 31), he writes with tears (2 Corinthians 2:4), all signs of his complete commitment to the Church. The epistle to the Hebrews reports that Jesus himself presented "prayers and supplications with tears" (Hebrews 5:7). Revelation finally promises comfort: God will wipe away every tear, concluding the journey of the word from human cry to divine consolation.
G1144.portee: The tear in the Bible is never a weakness, but a mark of emotional and spiritual depth. It reveals the authenticity of a relationship with God or with others: the tears of the sinful woman, of Paul the pastor, and even of Jesus in prayer show that a true heart allows itself to be transformed. For the Christian reader, meditating on the tear invites one not to suppress emotion before God, but to let it lead to sincere repentance and compassion for others. The final promise—that God will wipe away every tear—offers ultimate hope: our sorrows are not in vain; they will be transfigured by eternal comfort.

sens: To shed tears
To express sadness through tears
G1145.detail:
1. To shed tears: this is the physical and visible act of crying, allowing tears to flow from one's eyes. The word describes the concrete gesture, without specifying whether it is loud or silent.
2. To express sadness through tears: to cry is to manifest a deep feeling—sorrow, compassion, or intense emotion—through this natural means. In John 11:35, Jesus weeps at the death of Lazarus: it is the silent expression of authentic pain in the face of mourning.
G1145.origine: The verb comes from the root δακρύ-, related to the noun δάκρυον ("tear"). Greek uses this verb to translate the Hebrew בָּכָה ("to weep") in the Old Testament. Unlike other verbs of the same semantic family, δακρύω emphasizes the physical phenomenon of the tears themselves, rather than the cry or formal lamentation.
G1145.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament: John 11:35, the shortest verse in the Bible, where we are told that "Jesus wept." This context is one of mourning and compassion—Jesus weeps upon learning of the death of his friend Lazarus. The verb underscores the reality of Christ's human emotion in the face of death, without dramatizing through a loud cry or formal lamentation.
G1145.portee: This word reminds us that crying is human and good, even for Christ. Jesus does not hide his sorrow; he weeps at the sight of suffering and death. For the Christian reader, this verse legitimizes tears as an expression of love and compassion, and reveals a God who shares our emotions.

sens: jewelry in the shape of a circle worn on the finger
sign of honor, authority, or belonging
G1146.detail:
1. A ring is a piece of jewelry in a circular shape, usually made of metal, that is slipped onto the finger. It is the simplest and most common object to adorn the hands. In the parable of the prodigal son, the father orders his servants to put "a ring on the finger" of the returning son (Luke 15:22), alongside a beautiful robe and shoes.

2. In biblical culture, a ring is not only worn for beauty: it is also a symbol of honor, authority, or belonging to a person or household. By giving the ring to the prodigal son, the father signifies his total forgiveness, his restoration to the status of son, and his reintegration into the family with all honors.
G1146.origine: The Greek word δακτύλιος comes from the word δάκτυλος (daktylos), which means "finger." A ring is literally something that fits on the finger. In Hebrew, the Old Testament uses the word טַבַּעַת (tabaat), which also refers to this circle worn on the finger. The Greek word regularly translates this Hebrew term in the Greek translation of the Old Testament.
G1146.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: in Luke 15:22, in the parable of the prodigal son. It is a passage of forgiveness and restoration. The father, seeing his son return, orders that three things be given to him: a beautiful robe (symbol of dignity), shoes (symbol of the status of a free man), and a ring on his finger (symbol of power and belonging). Together, these three elements form a complete picture of the father's restoring grace.
G1146.portee: For the Christian reader, this ring in Jesus' words concretely illustrates what God's forgiveness means. It is not merely erasing a fault: it is fully restoring the person, returning their honor and status. Like the ring here, divine grace reintegrates the repentant sinner not as a servant, but as a beloved and honored child.

sens: Member of the human body, extension of the hand used for grasping and touching
Minimal action, insignificant effort
Manifestation of God's power
G1147.detail:
1. The finger is the small member that extends from the hand. Jesus heals the deaf-mute by putting "his fingers in the ears" (Mark 7:33), and the man at the resurrection recognizes Jesus by seeing "the fingers where the nails were" (John 20:25, 27). It is the most delicate and fine part of the body.
2. Figuratively, the finger represents the minimum of effort or gesture: the Pharisees "load men with burdens hard to bear, and do not touch with one of their fingers" (Luke 11:46) — in other words, they do not participate, not even with a little finger. The rich man in torment asks Abraham to send someone to "dip the tip of his finger in water" (Luke 16:24): a tiny gesture, but impossible.
3. Metaphorically, the "finger of God" refers to God's powerful action: Jesus says, "If I cast out demons by the finger of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you" (Luke 11:20). This shows that even the simplest gesture, when it comes from God, has immense power.
G1147.origine: The Greek word δάκτυλος comes from an ancient root meaning "to divide" or "to separate" — the finger separates and articulates the hand. In Hebrew, the word אֶצְבַּע (eṣba) has the same semantic field. The Greek word has retained its concrete and bodily meaning while also opening up to figurative use, particularly in the biblical expression "finger of God" to evoke divine intervention.
G1147.emploi: The word "finger" appears 8 times in the Gospels according to the Segond. It is used literally to refer to the body part: Jesus heals by touching (Mark 7:33), Jesus writes on the ground (John 8:6), and Thomas recognizes the Resurrected One by seeing his fingers (John 20:25, 27). Matthew and Luke use it figuratively to speak of minimal effort: the teachers of the Law load others but do not lift a finger (Matthew 23:4, Luke 11:46). Luke also uses the expression "finger of God" (Luke 11:20) to signify God's powerful action casting out demons, marking the irruption of the kingdom of God. Each use shows the importance of touch and gesture in Jesus' teaching.
G1147.portee: The finger reminds us that Jesus acts through touch: his physical presence and concrete gestures are essential to his healing ministry. When he asks the Pharisees why they refuse to move "even a little finger," he denounces hypocrisy and the lack of solidarity with the burdens of others. Finally, the "finger of God" shows us that even the simplest divine actions are signs of the present and active Kingdom.

sens: village or region on the shore of the Sea of Galilee
G1148.detail: Dalmanutha is a place located near the Sea of Galilee, in Galilee, the exact location of which is unknown to us today. Jesus goes there by boat with his disciples shortly after multiplying the loaves for the crowd (Mark 8:10).
G1148.origine: The name "Dalmanutha" is of Semitic origin, but its exact meaning has not been clearly established. Some relate this toponym to other place names in the region of the Jordan and the Sea of Galilee. The evangelist Matthew uses "Magdala" to apparently refer to the same place (Matthew 15:39), suggesting that these two names might refer to very close localities or the same region.
G1148.emploi: Dalmanutha appears only once in the New Testament, in Mark 8:10. Jesus arrives there after the multiplication of the loaves, at a moment when the disciples had seen him walking on water. This stop at Dalmanutha occurs before Jesus disputes with the Pharisees who come to ask him for a sign from heaven. The exact location remains mysterious and has never been definitively identified by archaeologists, unlike other Galilean villages.

sens: Ancient coastal region on the eastern shore of the Adriatic Sea
G1149.detail: Dalmatia is an ancient region located on the eastern coast of the Adriatic Sea, in what is called Illyria. It is a historical region of the Balkans, roughly corresponding to the coast of present-day Croatia. It is mentioned only once in the New Testament, in 2 Timothy 4:10, where the apostle Paul reports that Titus went there.
G1149.origine: The name "Dalmatia" comes from the ancient Greek Dalmatia (Δαλματία), itself derived from a local language of the Balkans. The ancient Greeks and Romans called it this to designate this important coastal region. The name has remained stable throughout history and still designates this region of the Balkans.
G1149.emploi: Dalmatia appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Timothy 4:10. The apostle Paul, writing to Timothy near the end of his life, mentions that Titus went to Dalmatia. At this point, Paul lists the destinations of various collaborators: Thessalonica, Galatia, and Dalmatia. This mention bears witness to the geographical expansion of Christian missionary activities beyond the main Mediterranean regions and to the more distant shores of the Adriatic.

sens: To submit a wild animal to obedience
To master a force or power that resists
To control what is untamable or difficult to restrain
G1150.detail:
1. To tame an animal means to make it docile, to submit it to the will of a man. In Mark 5:4, a man possessed by an evil spirit was so violent that no one had the strength to tame him, not even with chains. The verb evokes the effort required to domesticate a wild creature.

2. More broadly, to tame means to master a power or force that opposes us. James 3:7 states that all kinds of animals can be tamed by man — it is his ability to impose his will on creation.

3. In a figurative and moral sense, to tame means to master what normally escapes control. James 3:8 says that the tongue, no man can tame: it expresses the impossibility of controlling our words by our own strength.
G1150.origine: The verb comes from the Greek δάμη (the power to tame, authority) and evokes the image of one who breaks the resistance of an animal. In Hebrew, the word חֲשַׁל (Daniel 2:40) means "to crush, to destroy, to annihilate." The family of the Greek word includes δάμνημι (to be tamable) and illustrates the Greek contrast between nature (wild) and civilization (mastery).
G1150.emploi: The verb δαμάζω appears three times in the New Testament, always in Mark and James, and always in connection with what is difficult or impossible to control. In Mark 5:4, it describes the material impossibility of mastering a demoniac. In James 3:7, it serves to demonstrate man's power over animals — a commonplace fact, an obvious truth. But this contrast prepares the following verse (James 3:8) where the same verb, in the negative, reveals man's radical impotence in the face of his own tongue. The word thus shifts from the physical domain to the moral and spiritual domain.
G1150.portee: This word reminds us that man has received from God authority over creation (Genesis 1:28), but that he is himself limited: he can tame beasts, but not his own words. It is a lesson in humility about the limits of our mastery, and a call to recognize that only the grace of the Holy Spirit can truly restrain our tongue and our thoughts.

sens: Young female cow, particularly under three years old
G1151.detail: 1. A heifer is a young cow, still growing, before it has calved or reached full development. In Hebrews 9:13, Paul mentions "the ashes of a heifer" as part of the purification rite of the Old Covenant: these ashes, mixed with water, were sprinkled on the defiled Israelites according to the ritual described in Numbers 19. It is a simple and concrete image of what the Old Law could purify externally, in contrast to the sacrifice of Christ which purifies internally.
G1151.origine: The Greek word δάμαλις (damalis) is the feminine form of δαμάλης ("bullock"). It primarily translates the Hebrew פָּרָה (parah, "cow") and עֶגְלָה (eglah, "heifer"), both of which refer to female livestock. The word evokes the domesticated animal used in the religious rituals of the Old Testament.
G1151.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 9:13. The author of the Epistle to the Hebrews uses it to refer to the ritual prescriptions of purification of the Old Covenant. He mentions it alongside the blood of bulls and goats, as an animal sacrifice whose ashes had a legal purifying virtue. This reminder aims to show the insufficiency of the old rites compared to the perfect sacrifice of Christ.
G1151.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that the Old Covenant was based on external and material purifications, limited to "the purity of the flesh." In contrast, the death of Jesus Christ purifies the conscience and the soul entirely. This humble mention of a heifer underscores the transcendence of the salvation offered in Christ compared to the old observances.

sens: Woman from Athens converted to faith in Jesus
G1152.detail: Damaris is a woman living in Athens who listened to the apostle Paul preach on the Areopagus, the sacred hill where the wise and judges of the city gathered. Unlike most of her fellow citizens, she believed Paul’s message about Jesus Christ and attached herself to him to follow (Acts 17:34).
G1152.origine: The name Damaris comes from an ancient Greek root meaning "wife" or "woman." It is a classical Greek feminine name, rare in the New Testament where it appears only once.
G1152.emploi: Damaris is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Acts 17:34, during Paul's speech at the Areopagus in Athens. She is presented as one of the few people — along with Dionysius the Areopagite, a respected magistrate — who reacted with faith to the proclamation of the Gospel in this highly cultured and philosophical city. Her name is specifically reported, highlighting the importance of her individual conversion in the eyes of Luke, the author of Acts.
G1152.portee: Damaris embodies the transformative power of the Gospel that reaches even the hearts of the great cities of the ancient world, beyond cultural and intellectual barriers. Her named mention in Acts reminds us that every conversion matters in the eyes of God and the Church, and that faith can arise in the least predictable contexts.

sens: belonging to Damascus, coming from Damascus
concerning the governor or ethnarch of Damascus
G1153.detail: 1. This adjective qualifies what is originating from Damascus or belonging to it — the great city of Syria, the historical and commercial capital of the ancient Near East. In 2 Corinthians 11:32, Paul refers to "the ethnarch of King Aretas" who guarded the city: this is a Damascene magistrate, an officer responsible for Damascus.
G1153.origine: The Greek word Damaskēnos is formed from the name of the city Damascus (Δαμασκός). It is a simple adjective, of the type "of Damascus," as we would say "Lyonnais" for something coming from Lyon. It follows the usual Greek pattern for names of peoples and cities: adding a suffix (-nos for masculine, -nē for feminine, -non for neuter) to the name of the place.
G1153.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 11:32. Paul recalls a dramatic moment in his life: he had to flee Damascus because the ethnarch of King Aretas was searching for him, and his disciples lowered him in a basket through an opening in the wall. This Damascene ethnarch represents the civil and police authority of the city under Nabataean rule. The context shows Paul in danger, chased by local authorities — a narrative corroborated by the account in Acts 9:23-25, where it is a threat from the Jews of Damascus that he must flee.
G1153.portee: This word reminds Paul (and us) of a moment when his Christian life put him in direct peril: accused, hunted, humiliated even in his flight, he experienced physical vulnerability. For the reader, it provides a window into the reality of early Christianity: no easy triumph, but concrete trials, nocturnal escapes, risks taken for faith. This gives weight to the "sufferings" that Paul later enumerates (2 Corinthians 11:23-27).

sens: Capital city of ancient Syria
Center of Roman power in Syria
Site of Saul's conversion (the Apostle Paul)
Decisive stage in Paul's Christian life
G1154.detail:
1. Damascus is the capital of Syria, a large and important ancient city in the Near East. Paul was going there to persecute Christians when he had his vision of the Lord (Acts 9:2, 22:6).
2. The city was under Roman control at the time of the New Testament, with a governor established there to maintain order (2 Corinthians 11:32).
3. It was in Damascus that Saul had his transformative encounter with the risen Jesus: blinded by a heavenly light, he became an apostle and immediately began to preach Jesus in the synagogues of the city (Acts 9:19-27).
4. For Paul, Damascus marks the turning point of his life: from being a persecutor (he was going there to persecute), he returns to preach (Acts 9:27), which shows the radical change brought about by the Holy Spirit.
G1154.origine: Damascus comes from the Hebrew word *Dammèseq* (דַּמֶּשֶׂק), which also appears in the Old Testament as a major city of Syria. The Greek name *Damaskos* is the direct transliteration of this Hebrew term. Damascus is mentioned in the historical accounts of the Old Testament as a center of strategic and commercial importance.
G1154.emploi: Damascus appears fifteen times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in the Acts and letters of Paul (Acts 9, 22, 26; 2 Corinthians 11; Galatians 1). The passages describe Saul's journey to Damascus to persecute Christians (Acts 9:2), his miraculous conversion on the way (Acts 22:6), his stay and ministry in the city with the disciples (Acts 9:19-27), and his subsequent escape (2 Corinthians 11:32). Paul returns to it in his autobiographical account (Galatians 1:17), showing the importance of this place in his apostolic calling. Damascus is the scene of Saul's complete turnaround: from persecutor to preacher of the Gospel.
G1154.portee: Damascus symbolizes for every Christian the place where God can radically transform a life. Paul's story in Damascus shows that no one is too far from God, even one who fought against the Church. It is an encouragement: divine grace can seize the fiercest adversary and make him a servant. Damascus also reminds us that our conversion is a dateable and transformative event, and that witnessing fearlessly about Jesus in public is the first sign of a true encounter with the risen Christ.

sens: To give money to someone with the intention that they will repay it, often with interest
To borrow, meaning to receive money that one commits to repay
To lend generously, without expecting a return or gain
G1155.detail:
1. The fundamental meaning is to lend money with the expectation of being repaid, often with interest. Jesus says in Luke 6:34: "If you lend to those from whom you hope to receive, what credit is that to you?" — he refers here to the act of lending with the hope of a return.
2. The word can also mean to borrow, to receive a loan. In Matthew 5:42, Jesus says: "Do not turn away from the one who wants to borrow from you," where it is the debtor who acts.
3. In Luke, Jesus elevates the act of lending to a new level: "Lend without expecting anything back" (6:35). It is no longer a self-interested transaction, but a true gift, made out of love without calculating the return.
G1155.origine: The word comes from a Greek root related to borrowing and credit. The Greek Old Testament uses this verb to translate the Hebrew word meaning to borrow or lend. There is a synonymous verb, κίχρημι (kichrēmi), which expresses the act of lending among friends, without interest or commercial calculation — an important nuance for understanding the distinction that Jesus introduces in his teaching.
G1155.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, only in the Gospels of Matthew and Luke, in the context of Jesus' ethical teaching. In Luke 6:34, it describes ordinary and interested lending, that of sinners themselves. In Luke 6:35, Jesus transforms it into an act of radical charity — lending without expecting a return becomes a sign of resemblance to God who is good to the ungrateful. In Matthew 5:42, the verb in the passive form designates the one who borrows, emphasizing the believer's duty not to refuse.
G1155.portee: This word opens a door to the radical ethics of Jesus: it transforms a simple economic transaction into an act of selfless love. When we lend without expecting anything in return, we step out of the logic of exchange and enter into that of free giving, reflecting divine goodness. It is an invitation to examine our relationships with material goods and others: are we trapped in calculation, or freed by generosity?

sens: Money or goods borrowed, which must be repaid
Financial obligation, sum owed
G1156.detail:
1. A debt is a sum of money or a good that a person has borrowed from another and is committed to repay. It is the opposite of lending from the debtor's perspective: the one who must repay. In the parable of Matthew 18:27, a servant owes an enormous sum to the king and cannot pay; the king, moved with compassion, forgives (cancels) his debt.
2. The word more broadly designates any financial obligation, anything one owes to someone else. It is a contractual commitment: the one who has a debt has received something and is obligated to return or compensate for it.
G1156.origine: The Greek word δάνειον comes from the verb δανίζω (danizo), which means "to lend." The root evokes the act of giving something on loan, with the implicit expectation that it will be returned. In Hebrew, the Old Testament uses words like נָשָׁה (nasha) or עָבַט (avat) to designate debt, concepts that are very important in Mosaic law, which regulates loans and debt forgiveness.
G1156.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 18:27. It is part of the parable of the unforgiving servant, where Jesus teaches his disciples about limitless forgiveness. The "debt" here is both concrete (an enormous sum that the servant cannot pay) and metaphorical (it symbolizes the spiritual condition of every sinner before God). The king cancels the servant's debt in an act of mercy, which foreshadows the divine forgiveness that Jesus offers.
G1156.portee: This word reminds the believer that every sin against God is an "unpayable debt" that we can never repay by ourselves. Jesus uses this image to show that God's forgiveness is an act of pure, unmerited grace. It also invites the Christian to forgive as he has been forgiven, with the same generosity as the king towards his servant.

sens: one who lends money to someone
one who demands repayment of a debt
G1157.detail:
1. A creditor is a person who lends money to another person. They hold a right over the borrower: this money belongs to them and must be returned. This is exactly the case in the parable of Luke 7:41, where Jesus speaks of a creditor who lent money to two debtors, one owing five hundred denarii and the other fifty.
2. The creditor is also the one who demands, at the time of repayment, what is due to them. It is a relationship of debt: the creditor can be generous and forgive (as in the same parable), or strict and demand payment.
G1157.origine: The Greek word comes from the verb "to lend money" (δανείζω). It belongs to the family of words that describe commercial transactions and financial relationships. In ancient Greek, there are also related forms to designate lending and borrowing. It is a concrete word that reflects a daily reality of society: money transactions and debts.
G1157.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 7:41. Jesus uses it in a parable to teach about forgiveness of offenses. A creditor has two debtors: one owes a large sum (five hundred denarii), the other a small one (fifty denarii). The creditor forgives both their debts out of grace. This passage shows that the word is not neutral: it is used to illustrate mercy towards those who owe something.
G1157.portee: This parable of the merciful creditor invites the Christian to meditate on the forgiveness they have received from God. Just as this creditor canceled the debts, so God forgives the sins of those who believe in Jesus. It also calls for forgiving those who have offended us, in the image of this generous creditor. It is a profound lesson: our offenses against God resemble enormous debts that we could never pay, and forgiveness is an act of sovereign grace.

sens: The prophet who lived in Babylonian captivity and received visions from God about the future of the world
G1158.detail: Daniel is a Hebrew prophet who was deported to Babylon and served the kings of that kingdom. God granted him the gift of interpreting dreams and visions, and revealing hidden mysteries. He is particularly known for his apocalyptic visions concerning future kingdoms and the coming of the Messiah. In Matthew 24:15, Jesus himself cites him as a reliable prophet when speaking of "the abomination of desolation spoken of by the prophet Daniel."
G1158.origine: The Hebrew name דָּנִיֵּאל (Daniël) means "God is my judge" — composed of "El" (God) and "din" (to judge). This name expresses trust in divine justice. Daniel is the title held by this historical and prophetic figure from the Old Testament, whose book recounts his life, trials, and the visions received during the Babylonian exile.
G1158.emploi: Daniel appears twice in the New Testament, always cited by Jesus himself. In Matthew 24:15, Jesus refers his disciples to Daniel's prophecy about "the abomination of desolation." The same passage, reported in Mark 13:14, confirms that Jesus regarded Daniel's visions as essential prophecies for understanding the events of the end times. Jesus thus legitimizes Daniel's prophetic authority and uses it to prepare his disciples to recognize the signs of God's judgment.
G1158.portee: Jesus' mention of Daniel underscores the importance of Old Testament prophecies for the disciples. It teaches us that God speaks to his people in affliction and exile, and that his prophecies are fulfilled with certainty. For today's Christian, Daniel embodies faithfulness to God in a hostile world and the assurance that history is governed by the Most High, not by human powers.

sens: to exhaust one's money or resources by giving or consuming them
to use up everything one possesses
to invest or dedicate something for someone or a cause
to wear out, to tire oneself
G1159.detail:
1. To spend means to use and exhaust one's money or material goods by giving them to someone else or consuming them. The sick woman in Mark 5:26 "had spent all that she had" on doctors, until she had depleted her resources. This is the simplest and most common meaning of the word.

2. The word also describes the action of completely consuming, wasting, or dispersing all that one has. The prodigal son in Luke 15:14 "had spent everything," which means he had nothing left. This is a foolish expenditure, lacking wisdom.

3. To spend can also mean to provide for someone's expenses, to cover the costs or needs of another person. Paul, in Acts 21:24, asks to be able to "provide for the expenses" of the four men who are making a vow, meaning to pay what their religious act requires.

4. The word extends to the sense of giving oneself, exhausting oneself for others, as in 2 Corinthians 12:15 where Paul says: "I will very gladly spend... and be spent for your souls," meaning he will use all his strength and time in service to his converts.

5. To spend can also express the idea of consuming or satisfying: in James 4:3, the one who asks in order to "satisfy your passions" spends his money or energy to fulfill selfish desires.
G1159.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes the idea of spreading or dispersing. It belongs to the family of verbs that describe the act of using, consuming, letting escape. The Greek word carries the nuance of an expenditure that empties, that completely exhausts. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament (Septuagint), it is found in contexts where it concerns consuming or spending the resources of a person or a nation.
G1159.emploi: The verb "to spend" appears five times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Pauline epistles. It first describes material, concrete expenditures: the sick woman spent her money on doctors (Mark 5:26), the prodigal son squandered all his inheritance (Luke 15:14). The word then expands to more figurative uses: Paul "spends" his energy and life for the spiritual good of the churches (2 Corinthians 12:15), and one must "provide for the expenses" of those being supported (Acts 21:24). A final use designates an immoral expenditure: that which aims to satisfy personal passions (James 4:3). The context indicates whether the expenditure is wise, generous, foolish, or selfish.
G1159.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on the use of their resources: money, time, strength, talents. It teaches that spending for oneself alone, without wisdom, leads to ruin (the prodigal son), while spending for others in love is a sign of true Christian life (Paul). It highlights that self-giving is more precious than mere material almsgiving, and that true generosity does not hesitate to consume itself.

sens: The cost of an endeavor, what it requires in money or resources
What one must pay out, account for to carry out an action
G1160.detail:
1. The expense is the price to pay to accomplish something. It is the money necessary to complete a project. In Jesus' parable in Luke 14:28, the one who wants to build a tower must first sit down and calculate the expense — that is, assess how much it will cost in money and means.
2. More broadly, it is everything one must engage or sacrifice to accomplish something: not only money but also time, energy, and effort. The expense represents the price to pay, the real cost of an endeavor.
G1160.origine: The Greek word dapanē comes from a root that evokes the idea of spending, consuming a resource. It specifically designates what costs, what flows or is exhausted in achieving a goal. In the Greek versions of the Old Testament, it translates Aramaic or Hebrew words related to expenses and costs.
G1160.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 14:28, in a parable of Jesus about practical wisdom. Jesus uses it to call his listeners to reflection: before undertaking something great, one must first calculate, that is, realistically account for the expense it represents. It is a call to prudence and self-control in planning.
G1160.portee: This word from Jesus invites the disciple not to engage lightly on the path of faith. The word "expense" reminds us that following Jesus has a cost, that it requires total commitment. It is a call to count the cost, to be serious and realistic in our faith, without naivety — but also to accept this cost willingly, rather than abandoning along the way.

sens: coordinating conjunction linking two elements or two ideas
marks an opposition or contrast between two thoughts
introduces a new element in the narrative or reasoning
adds an explanation or clarification to what precedes
marks a logical continuity or consequence
G1161.detail:
1. This word simply connects two elements of the same level, like two links in a chain. In the genealogy of Christ (Matthew 1:3), it lists: "Judah begot Perez and Zerah by Tamar; Perez begot Hezron." The "and" links the names together without any particular nuance.
2. It can also mark an opposition or a turning point: after an affirmation, it introduces something contrary or unexpected. For example, when Jesus says to the healed woman: "Daughter, your faith has made you well" (Mark 5:34), the "but" that follows shows a change of direction or perspective in the discourse.
3. It often launches a new episode or scene, even if this new moment responds to the previous one. In John 21:1, "After this, Jesus revealed himself again to the disciples at the Sea of Tiberias": the "and" marks the transition to a new appearance of the Resurrected One.
4. Sometimes it slips in an explanatory parenthesis or adds a relevant detail without breaking the flow, as in 2 Corinthians 9:15 when giving thanks "for his indescribable gift."
5. It can also link a cause to its effect or a condition to its consequence, maintaining the logic of the discourse.
G1161.origine: This small particle is one of the most frequent words in the Greek of the New Testament, used more than 2500 times. It comes from very ancient and primitive roots of Greek. The corresponding Hebrew word (ו, waw) plays exactly the same role in the Old Testament: it connects words, phrases, and thoughts with remarkable flexibility. The absence of punctuation in ancient manuscripts made these particles essential for guiding the reader through the text.
G1161.emploi: This word appears about 2589 times in the New Testament, making it one of the most common conjunctions. It is found everywhere: in genealogies (Matthew 1), in miracle accounts, in Jesus' teachings, and in the letters of the apostles. Its use varies greatly depending on the context. Sometimes it simply links two statements without nuance (enumeration of facts), sometimes it marks a clear contrast ("you say this, but I say that"), and sometimes it shifts to a new scene or argument. In repetition, it can create an effect of insistence or solemn enumeration (as in the Beatitudes in Matthew 5). Its flexibility makes it an indispensable logical tool: it guides thought without stifling it.
G1161.portee: For the modern reader, this small particle is a key to biblical clarity. It shows how the authors of the New Testament thought and connected their ideas: no abrupt breaks, but a logical progression where each verse clings to the previous one. Learning to sense the nuances of "and" (simple connection, opposition, transitions, explanations) helps to better understand what the author really means. It is also a sign of the authenticity of the text: this particle is so natural in living speech that it reveals the voice of the disciples and apostles.

sens: A request expressed with insistence, addressed to someone more powerful
A heartfelt appeal, motivated by a need or distress
A prayer made to God, particularly at a moment when one feels a lack
G1162.detail: 1. Supplication is an urgent request, a plea made with urgency to someone who has the power to fulfill it. It is more than a simple request: it expresses a real need. In Luke 1:13, the angel tells Zechariah that his supplication has been heard: it was his request to have a child, expressed with the desire of the heart. 2. The word emphasizes the idea of lack, of a felt necessity. The one who supplicates recognizes that they are missing something and that they can only obtain it through this request. In Philippians 4:6, Paul urges to make known one's needs to God through prayers and supplications: it is expressing to God what we lack, what we need. 3. In the New Testament, supplication is always addressed to God. It is the prayer of the heart that cries out to God in recognition of its weakness and dependence on Him. In Hebrews 5:7, it is through supplications and tears that Christ, during his days of flesh, presented his requests to God.
G1162.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb δέομαι, which means "to need," "to lack." This verb expresses the idea of dependence and lack. Supplication carries this root within it: the one who supplicates acknowledges their need and insufficiency in relation to the one they address. In the Greek Old Testament, this word translates several Hebrew terms that denote the urgent cry of the heart toward God: the supplication, the cry of distress. It belongs to the same family as other forms of prayer, but it emphasizes the feeling of need and urgency.
G1162.emploi: The word δέησις appears 17 times in the New Testament, mostly in Paul's epistles. It is used to refer to requests made to God in prayer and fasting (Luke 2:37: Anna was constant in her supplications), as well as in moments of intercession for others (Romans 10:1: Paul expresses his supplication for the conversion of Israel; 2 Corinthians 9:14: the Macedonians pray for the Corinthians). Paul often links it to general prayer (Philippians 4:6: make known your needs through prayers and supplications), and it is among the forms of prayer he recommends (1 Timothy 2:1: prayers, supplications, intercessions). Unlike general prayer (προσευχή), supplication emphasizes the specific need that motivates the request.
G1162.portee: Supplication reminds the Christian that they are in a relationship of dependence on God: it is not a shame, but the reality of the human condition. It invites them to honestly express their needs and lacks to God, without fear. Far from being reserved for major issues, it can address the details of daily life. This prayer is also a form of love: interceding through supplication for others (like Romans 10:1) is to entrust them to God with sincerity.

sens: Express a logical or inevitable necessity, what must happen
Express a moral obligation or duty
Express a convenience or a condition appropriate to a situation
G1163.detail:
1. This meaning covers events that cannot not happen, because they are inscribed in God's design or in the nature of things. When Jesus tells his disciples that "it was necessary for him to go to Jerusalem" and that "he must suffer" (Matthew 16:21), he is not speaking of a mere plan: he asserts a necessity that is imposed upon him. Similarly, John the Baptist acknowledges: "He must increase, but I must decrease" (John 3:30), as if this order were inscribed in the order of the world.
2. The word also expresses a duty, an obligation that weighs on someone. When someone asks Peter: "What must I do to be saved?" (Acts 16:30), they seek to know the commandment, the obligatory action. The unfaithful servant should have placed the money "with the bankers, that at my coming I might have received what was my own with interest" (Matthew 25:27): that was his duty.
3. Sometimes, the word simply designates what is suitable, what is appropriate: "the hardworking farmer must be the first to partake of the crops" (2 Timothy 2:6), because it is in the nature of agricultural work that one must first toil to then harvest.
G1163.origine: The word comes from the verb "δέω" (deo), which fundamentally means "to be bound, to be tied." The basic idea is one of constraint or a bond: something binds you, ties you to an action or an event. That is why "δεῖ" expresses a necessity that weighs upon us, from which we cannot escape. In the Greek Old Testament, this verb often translates the obligation or appropriateness marked by the Hebrew context.
G1163.emploi: The word appears 105 times in the New Testament, especially in the Gospels and Acts. In Luke, it constantly recurs in the mouth of Jesus to affirm that his passion, death, and resurrection "must" occur according to Scripture (Luke 9:22, 17:25, 24:26, 24:46). In Acts, the apostles use it to express the inevitable nature of the divine plan or the duty to which they are subject (Acts 5:29, 17:3). Peter and Paul also use it for practical or moral obligations (2 Timothy 2:6). The word oscillates between raw necessity and the obligation that must be accepted.
G1163.portee: For the reader, this word reveals that the story of Christ is not due to chance or solely to human malice: it is part of a plan where the Father has placed a necessity that the Son freely accepts. This invites the believer to recognize, in the pressing events, not only obstacles or duties imposed from the outside but also a divine logic to which he can consent and participate.

sens: What is shown, presented for one to see
What serves as a model or reference
What warns by showing the consequences of a fault
G1164.detail: 1. The word first simply designates something that is shown, a specimen that is exhibited: it is the concrete image of the gesture of pointing to show. 2. It then designates a model, something placed before the eyes to be imitated or inspired by — good or bad. 3. But in biblical usage, "example" takes on a particular hue: it is an example of warning, a case that shows where sin leads and should instill fear. Sodom and Gomorrah are "set forth as an example" (Jude 1:7), that is, exposed as living proofs of God's judgment, so that others may fear and turn away from evil.
G1164.origine: The word comes from the verb δείκνυμι (to show, to make visible). It is from the same family as all words revolving around the idea of "showing": pointing, designating, making known. The suffix -μα forms nouns that denote the result of an action: an example is literally "something shown." In Hebrew, the word it often translates in the Greek Old Testament is one that means "warning" or "lesson" — something ostensible that should mark the minds.
G1164.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Jude 1:7. Jude uses it to qualify the fate of Sodom and Gomorrah: these cities have become an "example" because their spectacular destruction, their judgment by eternal fire, should serve as a warning to the readers. Jude cites this term to show that the God who judged the ancients will also judge the false teachers of his time. The example is not a mere model to imitate, but a terrifying demonstration of divine judgment — a case study of punishment.
G1164.portee: This word reminds the Christian that God's judgments are real and public: they are not hidden, but given "as an example" so that everyone understands the consequences of sin and turns away from it. It is an invitation to respectful fear and vigilance, not to paralyzing fear, but to clear obedience in the face of the warnings that God places before our eyes in Scripture.

sens: Show someone in public to dishonor them, put them on display
Subject someone to public ridicule, mock them
Manifest openly, make visible
G1165.detail:
1. The primary meaning of the word is to "make a spectacle" of someone by showing them to all eyes to cover them with shame. When Joseph refuses to "expose" Mary (Matthew 1:19), he chooses not to publicly shame her — because in Jewish law, making known the fault of a betrothed woman would have been to dishonor her before the entire community. The image is that of a humiliating display.
2. It is also the idea of a ridiculous or threatening exposure. In Colossians 2:15, Jesus "makes a spectacle" of the evil spiritual powers, exposing them to all, victorious, like a general who parades his enemies in a triumphal procession. The word carries the nuance of a publicly displayed victory.
3. Overall, "to expose publicly" can simply mean "to make visible," "to manifest"; but in the biblical context, this visibility almost always carries a shade of dishonor or triumph.
G1165.origine: The word comes from the Greek "déigma" (δεῖγμα), which means "example" or "spectacle." Adding the prefix and the verb changes the meaning: "to make into a spectacle," "to show as an example." The word is rare in biblical and classical Greek, making it a term chosen for its impact: exposing someone in this way is a serious action, worthy of note.
G1165.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In Matthew 1:19, it describes Joseph's refusal to publish the supposed shame of Mary — an act of justice and mercy, as he protects her from public condemnation. In Colossians 2:15, it designates Jesus' triumph over the powers of evil: he "makes a spectacle" of them, disarming and humiliating them definitively before the entire universe by his victory on the cross. The word shifts from a personal and private context to the cosmic context of Christ's victory.
G1165.portee: This word reminds us of the value of discretion and mercy: Joseph refuses to expose publicly; he prefers to protect. It also invites the Christian to see in Jesus the true victor, the one who unmasks and puts on display not men, but the forces of evil themselves. He embodies judgment and justice, but also the protection of those he loves.

sens: Present something to someone's view
Make known, reveal
Demonstrate, prove by facts
G1166.detail:
1. Presenting something to view means making it visible to someone, allowing them to see it with their own eyes. The resurrected Jesus "showed" his hands and side to the disciples so they could confirm his resurrection (John 20:20). The devil took Jesus to a mountain and "showed" him all the kingdoms of the world (Matthew 4:8). This is the most direct and common usage: putting something before someone's eyes.

2. Making known or revealing means communicating a hidden or spiritual reality. The angel said to John: "Come, I will show you the judgment of the great harlot" (Revelation 17:1), meaning he will help him understand, he will reveal this vision to him. God "shows" Moses the heavenly model of the tabernacle (Hebrews 8:5): he makes him see and know what he must build.

3. Demonstrating or proving means establishing the truth of something through facts or actions. James writes: "Show me your faith without works, and I will show you my faith by my works" (James 2:18) — each must prove their faith by acting on it. It is convincing through living proof.
G1166.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek and literally means "to point with a finger" or "to indicate." Its root evokes the primitive gesture of showing something with a finger to draw attention. In Hebrew, the verb "to show" often translates the verb "rāʾâ" (to see), particularly in its causative form which means "to make see." This continuity between showing and making see reveals the biblical thought: the one who shows something to someone brings them into knowledge.
G1166.emploi: This verb appears 31 times in the New Testament, primarily in the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John) and Revelation. It first denotes concrete gestures: showing a place, a road, one's wounds. Jesus "shows" signs and miracles (John 2:18), he "shows" his power through actions. But the word rises to spiritual meanings: God "shows" visions to his servants (Revelation 1:1, 4:1, 17:1), he "makes known" his plans to them. The verb can also mean "to show by proof": the apostle James uses it to speak of demonstrating one's faith through works. It is a word of revelation and manifestation, well-suited to the Scriptures.
G1166.portee: Understanding this verb enriches our biblical reading. When Jesus "shows" his resurrected wounds, it is an act of revelation intended to establish the faith of the disciples. When God "shows" a vision to a prophet or a truth to a believer, we learn that spiritual knowledge comes through divine revelation — it is not conquered alone. And when the text invites us to "show" our faith or love through our actions, it reminds us that true conviction must be seen, must manifest concretely.

sens: lack of courage, cowardice
paralyzing fear that prevents action
lack of self-confidence
G1167.detail:
1. Timidity is the lack of courage, a moral cowardice that makes one retreat in the face of danger or difficulty. It is not natural and healthy fear, but the inability to overcome fear to do what is right. In 2 Timothy 1:7, Paul categorically states that God has not given Timothy "a spirit of timidity" — he opposes this paralyzing weakness to the spirit of power, love, and wisdom.
2. Timidity is a fear that hinders action, an excessive reserve or restraint in the face of challenges or responsibilities. It renders one incapable of expressing oneself or moving forward with confidence.
3. It also expresses a lack of self-confidence and trust in God, doubt about one's own worth or the divine power that supports us.
