G1167.origine: The Greek word δειλία comes from the adjective δειλός ("cowardly," "timid"). It denotes the state or character of one who lacks courage. In Hebrew, it corresponds to several words expressing fear or dread (אֵימָה, מְחִתָּה), but with a much more negative connotation: it is not the reverential fear of God, but human cowardice that abandons trust.
G1167.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Timothy 1:7, where Paul uses it to reject a mindset that Timothy should not manifest. In this context of apostolic exhortation, Paul reminds his young disciple that his calling to preach and testify must not be paralyzed by timidity. On the contrary, God gives the spirit of power, love, and sound mind. The word stands in stark opposition to the confidence that the Christian must place in God and the firmness he must show in his faith.
G1167.portee: For the Christian, this word is a call to reject timidity as an obstacle to the life of faith. Paul teaches that God does not give us a spirit of paralyzing fear, but of power to witness and serve. Recognizing one's natural fear is one thing, but being dominated by timidity is another: it is doubting the presence and power of God within us. This warning encourages us to grow in confidence and to overcome our hesitations to fully live out our calling.

sens: to be troubled by fear, dread
to lose one's assurance in the face of danger or adversity
to manifest timidity or cowardice
G1168.detail:
1. To be alarmed means to be seized by fear or dread, to feel an anxiety that stirs the soul. It is the inner state of one who trembles before a threat or difficulty. Jesus tells his disciples in John 14:27: "Do not be alarmed."
2. The word also describes the loss of confidence and assurance in the face of what seems threatening. It is to abandon one's calm and firmness to succumb to anxiety, as when one fears an unfortunate event.
3. By extension, to be alarmed can express a form of cowardice or timidity — the weakness of one who retreats before trial instead of standing firm in faith.
G1168.origine: The word comes from the root δειλία (deilia), which denotes fear, timidity, cowardice. It is a verb formed from this adjective-noun, expressing the action of being taken by this fear. In the Greek texts that translate the Old Testament, this verb renders Hebrew words meaning "to tremble" or "to fear," such as חתת and פּחד, showing that to be alarmed is to physically and morally bend before fear.
G1168.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in John 14:27, in Jesus' last discourse to his disciples before his passion. Jesus exhorts them not to be alarmed — neither by the loss of his physical presence nor by the trials to come. It is a word of comfort and encouragement: he opposes the peace he gives to the natural fear that would seize them. The usage emphasizes that alarm arises from a lack of faith in the Lord's promise.
G1168.portee: This word speaks to the heart of the Christian. Jesus teaches us that alarm — anxiety, consuming worry — is not our lot if we receive his peace. It is not an invitation to indifference, but a call to entrust our fears to the one who loves us. Not to be alarmed is to choose to believe in the word of Christ rather than to yield to panic.

sens: Who is afraid, who fears
Who lacks courage, who does not dare to face danger
G1169.detail:
1. One who is afraid is seized with fear in the face of a threat or peril. When Jesus calms the storm, he reproaches his disciples for their fear: "Why are you afraid, you of little faith?" (Matthew 8:26). This is the same question in Mark 4:40. Fear paralyzes and prevents trust in God.
2. More broadly, it is the lack of courage — a moral weakness that prevents one from facing trials. In Revelation 21:8, the cowardly are listed among those who do not have the right to eternal life: "But as for the cowardly, the faithless, the detestable... their portion will be in the lake that burns with fire and sulfur." This cowardice reveals an absence of faith in God.
G1169.origine: The word comes from the Greek δέος (deos), "fear" or "terror." It is an adjective that describes one who is dominated by fear, who lacks courage. In Hebrew, the Greek Old Testament often translates terms like "weak" or "feeble" with this word, indicating a physical or moral weakness.
G1169.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament. In the first two passages (Matthew 8:26 and Mark 4:40), it describes the disciples' fearful reaction to the storm — a fear that contrasts with the faith they should have in Jesus. In the third passage (Revelation 21:8), cowardice becomes a sin that excludes from the Kingdom: it is one who refuses to testify or who abandons their faith out of fear of persecution. The word thus denotes both an emotion (fear) and a moral vice (lack of courage before God).
G1169.portee: This word challenges the Christian regarding their fears and courage. The disciples are afraid even though Jesus is with them: the text invites us to recognize that our fears often reveal a lack of trust in God. In Revelation, cowardice is not presented as a fatality, but as a position of the heart — that of one who, out of fear of the world, denies their faith. It is a call to trust and faithfulness, even in trials.

sens: an unspecified person referred to without naming them
G1170.detail: 1. "Such" refers to a person who cannot or does not want to be named precisely. It is a vague way of speaking, leaving the name in the shadows. In Matthew 26:18, Jesus tells his disciples to go to "such a one" to prepare the Passover: he does not give the name of the owner of the house, as that is not important for the narrative — only that they find the place of the feast.
G1170.origine: The Greek word δεῖνα comes from a root meaning what is manifest or visible, but it has developed the opposite sense: that of something pointed out without being named, designated vaguely, as if pointing with a finger and saying "that guy there." It is a rare word in classical and biblical Greek, used when one wants to remain deliberately vague.
G1170.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 26:18. Jesus gives the disciples cryptic instructions to prepare the Passover meal: instead of naming the owner of the house, he simply says "such a one." This vagueness is intentional — Jesus likely wants to prevent Judas from discovering the exact location before the right moment. It is a typically narrative usage, serving to preserve a secret or discretion.
G1170.portee: This small word reminds us that in the Gospel, Jesus sometimes speaks with hidden wisdom: he does not tell everything to everyone, and he protects what must be protected. For the reader, this invites trust: even when we do not understand all the details of God's plan, we can rely on his wisdom and timing.

sens: In a serious, intense, and painful way
In an impetuous and hostile manner
G1171.detail:
1. The word describes a deep and overwhelming suffering or distress. The centurion's servant in Matthew 8:6 suffers "terribly" from paralysis: it is a physical agony that torments the one who endures it.
2. It can also qualify an aggressive and vehement pressure, a relentless pursuit. In Luke 11:53, the scribes and Pharisees begin to "press violently" against Jesus: they harassed him insistently and maliciously, bombarding him with questions to trap him.
G1171.origine: The word comes from the Greek root δέος (deos), which expresses fear and dread. "Terribly" thus carries the idea of what inspires fear or horror. The adverb adds to this feeling the idea of intensity: not only is it frightening, but it is in an extreme manner that seizes and torments.
G1171.emploi: This word appears only twice in the New Testament according to the Segond. In Matthew 8:6, it qualifies the physical suffering of the centurion's paralyzed servant: the ailment he suffers from is intense and painful. In Luke 11:53, it describes the hostile attitude of the scribes and Pharisees towards Jesus: they pressed him with malicious fervor, multiplying questions to accuse him. In both cases, the word emphasizes an intensity that is both painful for the one who endures it and, in the second case, threatening.
G1171.portee: This word helps us understand the gravity of human suffering and the importance of Jesus' compassion. The centurion presents his servant as suffering "terribly," and Jesus heals him immediately, showing that nothing escapes his love. It also shows us how religious opposition to Christ can take aggressive and relentless forms: the Gospel does not avoid tensions, but invites us to remain faithful despite harassment.

sens: To have the main evening meal
To participate in a meal, to eat together
To share the intimacy of communion
G1172.detail:
1. The verb refers to the action of having the evening meal, called "supper" in French. It is the main meal of the day in the Greco-Roman world. In Luke 17:8, the master asks his servant to prepare the supper before the master himself eats.

2. In a context of conviviality, "supper" expresses the act of sharing a meal, of being seated at the table together. The emphasis is on the act of eating together rather than merely filling the stomach. In 1 Corinthians 11:25, Paul reminds that Jesus "after having supped" took the cup: it is the moment of the meal, the context of intimacy and sharing.

3. In a figurative and spiritual sense, "supper" evokes a deep communion, an intimate presence. In Revelation 3:20, Jesus promises: "I will come in to him and eat with him, and he with me" — the verb is no longer simply to eat, but to share a personal and warm communion.
G1172.origine: The verb derives from the noun δεῖπνον (deipnon), which means "evening meal." It does not have a clearly identifiable Indo-European root in Greek: it is a rather isolated word that specifically designates dinner or supper. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament (used by early Christians), the word occasionally renders the Hebrew לחם (lechem, "bread," by extension "meal"). The Greco-Roman cultural context — where supper is the main and convivial meal of the day — explains why this word has an emotional charge: it is a time of relaxation, family, and friends.
G1172.emploi: The verb appears 4 times in the New Testament, always in the Gospels or Paul. In Luke 17:8 and 22:20, it situates an action in a context of service or meal ceremony. In 1 Corinthians 11:25, Paul takes it up while recounting the institution of the Supper: Jesus "after having supped" took the cup. This mention of the ordinary evening meal emphasizes that the moment was a real moment of intimacy, not a theatrical display. In Revelation 3:20, the context becomes metaphorical: Jesus does not announce a material meal, but promises to enter into personal and warm communion with the one who opens their heart to him. The verb retains this nuance of sharing and conviviality everywhere.
G1172.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that the simplest gestures — eating together, sharing a meal — are loaded with spiritual meaning. The Supper is not an abstract ceremony, but the continuation of the moment when Jesus broke bread with his disciples in intimacy. And the promise in Revelation 3:20 affirms that friendship with Jesus is real, personal, warm — a communion that transforms the ordinary into the sacred.

sens: The main meal of the day, taken in the late afternoon or evening
A gathering of diners around the table, a festive occasion
A banquet or official feast
Figuratively, a great celebration or communion
G1173.detail:
1. The supper was the main daily meal for Jews at the time (unlike our breakfast). It was taken in the afternoon or evening, at home or at someone else's place. Jesus said to the man who invited him: "A man gave a great supper, and invited many" (Luke 14:16) — it is an evening meal meant to gather guests.
2. The word also refers to the complete social event: the gathering of diners at the table, the moment of feasting together. The Pharisees "love the best seats at feasts" (Matthew 23:6) — they seek the honor of being seated near the host during the meal.
3. A supper can be a reception or a more formal banquet, with numerous guests and preparation. Herod organized one to celebrate his birthday (Mark 6:21).
4. Revelation speaks of the "marriage supper of the Lamb" (Revelation 19:9) and the "great supper of God" (Revelation 19:17): these images refer to the final communion, the heavenly celebration, the eternal communion of Christ with His people.
G1173.origine: The Greek word deipnon comes from a root meaning the action of eating or nourishing oneself. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), it mainly translates Hebrew words referring to a meal or a banquet. It is a simple and common word in Greek and Roman culture, carried over into the New Testament because it exactly corresponds to the reality of the Jewish evening meal.
G1173.emploi: The word appears 16 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John) and twice in Revelation. It primarily describes ordinary suppers or receptions: Jesus is invited to a supper at a Pharisee's house (Luke 14:16 speaks of a great supper), or at Lazarus' house in Bethany (John 12:2). The Pharisees are shown seeking the best seats at feasts (Matthew 23:6, Mark 12:39) — a detail about their vanity. The crucial moment of Jesus' last meal with His disciples is also called the supper (John 13:2, 4), where He washes the feet of His disciples. In 1 Corinthians 11:20-21, Paul speaks of the "Lord's supper," the Lord's meal (the Eucharist), and denounces those who selfishly eat at that time. Finally, Revelation uses the image of the supper figuratively twice: the "marriage supper of the Lamb" and the "great supper of God," symbolizing Christ's final reign and judgment.
G1173.portee: This word reminds us that Jesus shared meals with His disciples and friends, where He communicated with them: the meal is not just a physical necessity, it is a moment of intimacy and communion. The biblical image of the supper—particularly the "Lord's supper"—invites the Christian to see every meal taken in community, and especially the Communion, as an opportunity to join with Christ and His people. Biblical eschatology itself uses the language of the supper to speak of the final and eternal joy in the presence of the Lord.

sens: Who fears the divinity and worships it
Who observes religious practices with respect
Who is devoted to the gods or to God
G1174.detail:
1. The word describes someone who has fear towards the divinity and worships it: it is an attitude of reverence towards divine powers. When Paul arrives in Athens, he observes that the Athenians are "very religious" (Acts 17:22), meaning they show respect for the gods and practice worship towards them.
2. More broadly, the word characterizes one who observes religious practices seriously and respectfully, who takes duties towards the gods seriously. It is a piety that manifests in actions and attitudes.
3. The word can also emphasize a conscious and intentional devotion towards the divinity, a form of religious respect that goes beyond indifference.
G1174.origine: The word combines two Greek roots: δείδω, which means "to fear," and δαίμων, "divinity." The initial image is that of fear before the gods. This combination shows that religiosity, for the Greeks, arises from a respectful fear of divine powers. The word belongs to the family of words expressing piety and religious respect.
G1174.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 17:22. Paul uses it to compliment the Athenians regarding their general religious attitude, observing that they are very attentive to worships and altars. In this context, the term describes a certain religious concern, although this religiosity is directed towards multiple gods and, from a Christian perspective, towards idols. The word does not carry a negative connotation in itself, but highlights the extent and sincerity of religious practice.
G1174.portee: This passage reminds the Christian that the religious desire and spiritual quest are deeply rooted in the human heart, even among those who do not know the true God. Paul acknowledges this Athenian piety while calling them to turn to the living God whom they seek without knowing it. This invites the Christian reader to see in human religiosity a trace of the aspiration to God, while understanding that only a relationship with the God revealed in Christ truly satisfies this spiritual thirst.

sens: Reverential fear towards the gods, religious respect
The set of religious practices and beliefs
Piety, sincere attachment to God
Superstition, unfounded religious beliefs
G1175.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the attitude of respectful fear towards the divinities: it is the fear of the gods, not the kind that paralyzes, but the kind that drives one to honor them and follow their rules. In Acts 25:19, it is used to refer to the debates of the Jews with Paul regarding "their religion," meaning their particular religious practices and beliefs.
2. Concretely, the term can also refer to the entirety of observances, rites, and doctrines that form a religious system — religion as a visible and organized phenomenon.
3. By extension, it can express true piety: sincere and reverential attachment to God that guides moral and spiritual conduct.
4. Nevertheless, the word can take on a pejorative nuance and denote superstition: a fear of the gods that is not based on truth or true knowledge, but on irrational fears or unfounded practices.
G1175.origine: The Greek word δεισιδαιμονία comes from δεῖσος (fear) and δαίμων (divinity, divine spirit), which literally means "fear of divine spirits." It is a compound that evokes the idea of respecting or fearing supernatural powers. In Greek thought, this word oscillated between two poles: on one side admirable piety, on the other unreasonable superstition. The context and the speaker's intention determined the judgment.
G1175.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 25:19. In this passage, Festus describes to Agrippa II how Paul had discussions with the Jews about questions of "religion," particularly concerning the question of Jesus. Here, the term is neutral: it simply denotes the religious divergences between Paul and his Jewish opponents, without positive or negative connotation. The context shows that Festus, a Roman governor, sees this religious dispute as typical of the Jewish questions he must manage.
G1175.portee: This word reminds us that religion is primarily a matter of respectful fear towards God, a wonder before His power and authority. For the Christian, this means that true piety is not primarily a matter of external rules, but of sincere reverence towards the living God. At the same time, the ambiguity of the term in the Greek language warns the biblical reader: any religious practice without a true foundation in the knowledge of God risks becoming superstition.

sens: The number 10, cardinal digit representing this quantity
By extension, a group or set of ten units or ten people
Figures a short or limited period in duration
G1176.detail:
1. The word δέκα simply designates the number ten, understood as a numerical quantity: it is the digit we use in calculation and counting. In the parable of Luke 15:8, the woman possesses ten drachmas (coins) and loses one; in the parable of the talents in Luke 19:16, a servant receives ten minas to manage and brings back ten more.
2. The word can designate a specific group or set of ten people or ten things. In Matthew 20:24, "the ten" apostles are indignant against James and John; in Luke 17:12, ten lepers come to meet Jesus.
3. By its nature as a round and complete number, ten can represent a brief and determined period or duration. In Revelation 2:10, the "tribulation of ten days" signifies a limited and short trial, not eternal: "You will have tribulation for ten days."
G1176.origine: The word δέκα comes from an ancient common Indo-European root shared by Greek, Latin (decem), and French (dix). In Hebrew, the number ten is expressed by עשרה (asara). It is a fundamental number in ancient counting, often used to form a complete cycle or a basic unit.
G1176.emploi: The word appears 24 times in the New Testament, primarily in the Gospels and Revelation. It is used concretely: to count people (the apostles in Matthew 20:24, the lepers in Luke 17:12), goods (minas or drachmas in the parables of Luke 19 and Luke 15:8), or visionary elements (the ten horns of the beast in Revelation 17:3 and 17:12). In apocalyptic texts, the number ten takes on a more symbolic value: the ten horns represent a totality of foolishly hostile power, while "ten days" of affliction in Revelation 2:10 signifies a trial that will have an end.
G1176.portee: The number ten reminds the Christian reader that even in trials and tribulations, God sets a limit to what we must endure. The parables where ten appears (the ten drachmas, the ten minas) teach the responsibility of faithfully managing what God entrusts to us, no matter how modest it may be. It is a number of completeness that invites trust: what is complete can also be accomplished and finished.

sens: the number 15
distance measured in stadia
duration measured in days
G1178.detail:
1. Fifteen is the whole number that comes after fourteen and before sixteen. It is a numeral adjective, like "ten" or "twenty," used for counting or enumerating.
2. When measuring a distance in stadia (an ancient Greco-Roman unit of length), fifteen stadia designates a precise distance: John 11:18 uses it to say that Bethany was about fifteen stadia from Jerusalem.
3. When measuring a depth in fathoms (length of the outstretched arm), fifteen fathoms indicates a precise depth: in Acts 27:28, Paul and his companions take soundings and first find twenty fathoms, then fifteen fathoms as they approach land.
4. When counting days, fifteen days is a duration: Galatians 1:18 recounts that Paul stayed fifteen days in Jerusalem with Cephas (Peter) to get to know him.
G1178.origine: The Greek word is formed from two elements: δεκα (deca, "ten") and πέντε (pente, "five"). It is a recent form of Greek to say "ten and five." The older form was πεντεκαίδεκα (pentekaideca), but δεκαπέντε became the common way to count this number.
G1178.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, always to state a precise number in a practical way. In John 11:18, it measures a distance between two villages (Bethany and Jerusalem) so that the reader understands they were close to each other. In Acts 27:28, it measures the depth of the sea: Paul and his companions approach land and measure the depth twice — first twenty fathoms, then fifteen fathoms — showing they are getting closer to shore. In Galatians 1:18, it quantifies a duration: Paul stays fifteen days with Peter, highlighting the brevity and importance of this meeting for establishing his apostleship.
G1178.portee: This word reminds us that concrete numbers in the Bible (distances, depths, days) are never arbitrary: they help the reader visualize events and grasp their significance. The fifteen stadia between Bethany and Jerusalem show that Jesus had withdrawn very close, the fifteen fathoms in Acts emphasize the approach to the promised land, and the fifteen days with Peter mark a pivotal moment in Paul's life.

sens: region made up of ten cities
territory east of the Jordan
Hellenized area of Syria-Palestine
G1179.detail:
1. The Decapolis is a region composed of ten cities (its Greek name means "ten cities"), located east of the Jordan, in the territory known as Transjordan. These cities formed a commercial and political league under Roman rule.

2. It is a territory strongly marked by Greek and Roman culture, unlike the strictly Palestinian Jewish regions: Greek was predominantly spoken there, and pagan gods were honored. When Jesus travels there, he enters a world very different from that of Jerusalem or Galilee.

3. In the Gospels, the Decapolis appears as a place where the good news of Jesus spreads widely: the man healed from the legion of demons (Mark 5:20) "began to proclaim in the Decapolis all that Jesus had done for him," and the account indicates that "everyone was amazed."
G1179.origine: The Greek name "Dekapolis" combines the word "deka" (ten) and "polis" (city). It was not a Hebrew name, but a Greek designation for a confederation of cities that historically formed after the conquest of Alexander the Great. These cities maintained relative autonomy while being subject to the Roman Empire.
G1179.emploi: The Decapolis is mentioned three times in the synoptic Gospels. In Matthew 4:25, it is listed among the regions from which the crowds that follow Jesus at the beginning of his ministry come — it is mentioned alongside Galilee, Jerusalem, and Judea, showing that its influence was widespread. In Mark 5:20 and Mark 7:31, it is the place where Jesus performs miracles and where his fame spreads. These passages show that Jesus did not limit his ministry to Jewish Palestine but also engaged in these pagan and Hellenophone regions.
G1179.portee: The mention of the Decapolis reminds the reader that the gospel was not only addressed to Jews but also to non-Jews and pagans. It is a sign that salvation in Jesus Christ transcends ethnic and religious boundaries and extends to all peoples, in all cultural contexts.

sens: the number 14
a period or interval of 14 years
a series or succession of 14 generations
G1180.detail:
1. Fourteen is simply the number 14, used for counting or enumerating. In Matthew 1:17, Matthew divides the history of the people of Israel into three groups of fourteen generations: from Abraham to David, from David to the exile, and from the exile to Christ. This division reveals the divine structure of salvation history.
2. Fourteen can also refer to a duration of 14 years. Paul recounts in Galatians 2:1 that he went up to Jerusalem "fourteen years later" after his conversion, marking a significant interval in his missionary life. Similarly, in 2 Corinthians 12:2, he mentions a mystical experience that occurred "fourteen years" earlier.
3. The number 14 can organize a genealogy or a series. Matthew makes it a structuring principle: each group of fourteen generations marks a major milestone in God's plan for His people.
G1180.origine: The Greek word δεκατέσσαρες (fourteen) is composed of two elements: déca- ("ten") and tessares ("four"), literally "ten-four." It is the common form in late Greek and modern Greek for all numbers beyond thirteen. The older classical form was tessareskaidéka, but dékatessares gradually became established. This word translates the Hebrew arba'ah-'asar with the same composition: "four-ten."
G1180.emploi: The word appears three times in the provided New Testament, always with a concrete meaning. In Matthew 1:17, Matthew organizes the genealogy of Christ into three sections of fourteen generations: this numerical structure is not insignificant—it highlights the regularity and order of the divine plan. In Galatians 2:1 and 2 Corinthians 12:2, Paul uses fourteen to measure significant time intervals: fourteen years after his conversion before seeing the apostles, and fourteen years before recounting a mystical vision. In these three contexts, the number 14 functions as a marker of a significant moment or period in salvation history or in Paul's life.
G1180.portee: For the Christian reader, the number 14 in Matthew reveals that the story of salvation is not the result of chance, but follows an order intended by God. Each generation has its place in the divine plan that culminates in Christ. In Paul's case, the periods of fourteen years mark mature and decisive stages: conversion, deep spiritual experience, confirmation of apostleship. This number invites us to see God's hand at work in the measurable time of our own lives.

sens: The part that is one-tenth of the total
A religious tax of one-tenth of income or spoils
A portion as an ordinal number in a series
G1182.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the mathematical fraction: one-tenth of the whole. In Revelation 11:13, it literally refers to "the tenth part of the city" that collapses during the earthquake.
2. It is also the religious tax, the offering due to God and His servants. Abraham gives "the tithe of the spoils" to Melchizedek (Hebrews 7:4), thus acknowledging the spiritual superiority of this priest of the Most High. This tithe is a mark of submission and respect towards one who is greater.
3. It can also refer to the order of rank in a series: John 1:39 speaks of "the tenth hour," meaning the time of day when ten hours have passed since dawn.
G1182.origine: The word comes from the Greek δέκα (ten). It corresponds in Hebrew to מַעֲשֵׂר (maassar), which also means tenth and tithe. This notion of a tenth part offered to God dates back to the origins of the Old Testament, where it expressed God's right over human labor and the duty of the people to honor God through this gift.
G1182.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the New Testament, primarily in the epistle to the Hebrews and in Revelation. Hebrews 7 uses it three times to recount how Abraham paid the tithe to Melchizedek, God's priest; this passage establishes that giving a tithe means recognizing the superior spiritual dignity of the recipient. John 1:39 uses it to indicate the time of day (the tenth). Revelation 11:13 speaks of a portion or part, then Revelation 21:20 continues this enumeration. The meaning nuances between the arithmetic fraction, the cultic offering, and the ordinal number.
G1182.portee: The tithe is an act of worship and recognition of God's right over our possessions. Abraham, the father of believers, humbles himself by giving the tithe to the one who brings him a blessing, showing that offering a portion to God is natural and right for a submitted heart. It reminds us that everything we possess comes from God and belongs to Him.

sens: To take a tithe, that is, one-tenth of the harvest or income
To collect this tenth from someone, to demand it from them
To pay one's own due tithe
G1183.detail:
1. The verb δεκατόω comes from the Greek word for "ten" and denotes the action of taking a tithe, one-tenth. In the biblical context, it is the system by which a person would give one-tenth of their income or harvest—a well-established religious and legal practice in Israel. Melchizedek "takes the tithe" from Abraham (Hebrews 7:6), meaning that Abraham gives him this tenth.
2. The verb can also describe the side of the one who demands this tithe: to collect the tenth from someone else, to compel them, or to receive it. It is the action of the priest or collector who goes to seek this religious tax from the people.
3. In the passive form, the verb means "to pay the tithe," "to settle what one owes in tithe." Abraham "pays the tithe" through Levi (Hebrews 7:9): he recognizes this obligation to Melchizedek through his descendant Levi, who as a priest will himself receive the tithes from other Israelites.
G1183.origine: The word δεκατόω is formed from δεκάτη (the tithe, the tenth) and the verbal suffix -όω which makes it a verb. The tithe itself comes from the Greek word for "ten," expressing the idea of a proportional deduction: one part out of ten. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, the corresponding verb is עשׂר (ʿaśar) in the causative form, with the same meaning of "to take a tithe." This religious practice dates back to the origins of Israel and symbolizes the recognition that all goods come from God.
G1183.emploi: The verb δεκατόω appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Hebrews 7, in a passage that relies on the story of Melchizedek in Genesis 14. Hebrews 7:6 recalls that Melchizedek took the tithe from Abraham, thus establishing the superiority of this priest who foreshadows Christ. Hebrews 7:9 uses the passive form to affirm that Abraham, although an ancestor of Levi (future priest), somehow paid the tithe through his descendant, implicitly recognizing Melchizedek's superiority. This verb is therefore used to demonstrate the greatness of Jesus Christ as a priest "in the order of Melchizedek."
G1183.portee: This word invites us to reflect on the tithe and the principle of religious giving. It shows that the tithe was not a late or arbitrary invention, but rooted in the recognition of each believer's relationship to God and His promises. For a Christian reader today, it reminds us that the act of giving a portion of our goods to the work of God is an ancient and significant gesture, expressing our dependence on God and our commitment to Him.

sens: That which pleases, received with satisfaction
That which is suitable, timely
That which deserves to be approved, accepted
G1184.detail:
1. Pleasing: that which pleases someone, that which suits them and is willingly received. When the Segond translates "grace" in Luke 4:19 ("the year of the Lord's favor"), it refers to the year when God is favorable, when He looks upon with kindness. In Philippians 4:18, the offering of the Philippians is "pleasing" to God — it pleases Him, He receives it with satisfaction.
2. Favorable, timely: the word also evokes what happens at the right moment, what suits the circumstance. In 2 Corinthians 6:2, the "favorable time" is the moment when God listens and saves — the moment when His door is open.
3. Worthy of acceptance: he who fears God and practices righteousness is "pleasing" to Him (Acts 10:35) — this is someone whom God approves and receives, regardless of their nation or past.
G1184.origine: This word comes from the Greek verb to receive or welcome (δέχομαι). Its underlying image is that of a welcoming gesture: when one receives something or someone with open arms, they judge it acceptable. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew word meaning will or divine favor.
G1184.emploi: The word appears five times in the New Testament, concentrated in Paul's epistles and in Acts. In Luke 4:19, Jesus quotes the prophecy of Isaiah about "the year of favor," a jubilee year when God delivers the oppressed. In Acts 10:35, Peter declares that every man who fears God, regardless of his nation, is "pleasing" in His sight — a turning point in the understanding of the Gospel open to all. In 2 Corinthians 6:2, it is the moment when God answers, when His kindness is exercised. In Philippians 4:18, Paul thanks the Philippians: their gift is "pleasing" to God, received as a delightful fragrance. The meaning oscillates between divine grace (God's favor) and acceptability (that which deserves to be received).
G1184.portee: This word speaks of God's grace as active favor: there are times and moments when God shows kindness and answers those who seek Him. It also reminds us that our obedience and offerings are only received if they please God — not out of deserved pride, but by His benevolent disposition. It is a word of freedom and hope: the oppressed can be freed in the time of His favor; everyone, without distinction, can be pleasing to God if they fear Him and act justly.

sens: To attract by bait (in a literal or figurative sense)
To seduce by promises or desires
To gradually lead towards evil
G1185.detail:
1. The word comes from the image of the bait placed on a hook to catch fish: it is primarily to attract someone by offering something desirable. In 2 Peter 2:14, false teachers "entice unstable souls" by drawing them towards sin as one attracts fish.
2. To entice is to seduce by presenting something appealing: the desires of the flesh, easy promises. In 2 Peter 2:18, the seducers "entice by the desires of the flesh" those who are not yet firm in faith.
3. The word also describes the process where personal desire gradually leads us towards evil: in James 1:14, each one "is drawn away and enticed by his own desire," like a fish that bites the hook of sin.
G1185.origine: The Greek word δελεάζω comes from δέλεαρ, which literally means the bait placed on a hook or fishing line. The word retains this sensory image: to attract by something tempting. It is an action verb, describing the moment when one puts out the bait or seduces.
G1185.emploi: The verb appears only three times in the New Testament, always in the context of sin and temptation. In James 1:14, Paul (or James) uses it to describe the internal mechanism of temptation: it is our own desire that entices us. In 2 Peter 2:14 and 2:18, Peter denounces the false teachers who "entice" unstable young Christians, meaning they intentionally seduce them by drawing them towards carnal desires. The word emphasizes the insidious and gradual aspect of seduction.
G1185.portee: This word helps us understand two realities of temptation. First, that sin functions like bait: it attracts us by offering something seemingly desirable. Second, that we are not just passive victims — in James 1:14, it is our own desire that entices us. This warns us against false teachers who exploit this vulnerability to seduce Christians who are not yet mature in faith.

sens: woody plant with a trunk, branches, and leaves
to produce fruit (good or bad)
symbol of life or the moral work of a person
the entirety of created beings, in a cosmic vision
G1186.detail:
1. The word simply designates the tree as a plant: it is found in descriptive or concrete passages, such as when Jesus speaks of cutting branches from trees (Matthew 21:8), or in apocalyptic visions where trees are creatures to be protected (Revelation 7:3).

2. The tree is primarily a moral symbol: a good tree bears good fruit, a bad tree bears bad fruit (Luke 6:43). It is the nature of the heart that reveals itself through actions — as the fruit betrays the quality of the tree. Jesus asserts that "a good source naturally produces good actions."

3. In parables, the tree represents the spiritual state of a person or their ministry: a fruitless tree must be cut down and thrown into the fire (Matthew 7:19), an image of divine judgment on spiritual barrenness. It is a pressing invitation to bear fruit in the Christian life.

4. In Revelation, trees appear as an integral part of the entire creation: God protects "the trees" alongside the earth and the sea (Revelation 7:3), revealing that the created world has value and will be renewed.
G1186.origine: The Greek word dendron comes from a root that designates that which grows, that which sprouts. It translates the Hebrew etz, which has the same concrete and figurative meaning: the tree as a living reality and as an image of fertility or destruction. It is a simple and natural word from everyday vocabulary.
G1186.emploi: The word appears 18 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Revelation. Jesus frequently uses it in moral teaching: the good tree and the bad tree (Matthew 7:17-18, Luke 6:43-44) illustrate the principle that inner nature inevitably manifests through outward acts. The idea of judgment arises when the tree does not produce fruit (Matthew 3:10, Luke 3:9) — this is the fate of barrenness. In parables, a small tree can grow remarkably (Matthew 13:32, Luke 13:19). Revelation broadens the scope: the trees there are created realities under divine protection, threatened by eschatological plagues.
G1186.portee: This word invites the believer to examine the "fruit" of their own life: what actions, what words, what relationships truly reveal their spiritual nature? It also teaches that God judges not appearance or pretense, but inner reality. Finally, it reminds us that all creation — including trees — belongs to God and will be renewed in His kingdom.

sens: Soldier armed with a spear or javelin
Fighter capable of handling a projectile weapon
Light warrior attached to the protection of an officer
G1187.detail:
1. The word designates a type of soldier equipped with a projectile weapon, probably a short spear or javelin. The emphasis is on martial dexterity: it is a man trained to strike the enemy from a distance, with particular precision. In Acts 23:23, Paul is escorted by Roman lancers among other troops (cavalry, infantry): these are specialized soldiers, probably battle-hardened.
2. More broadly, the term designates any fighter equipped for close combat with a projectile weapon — javelin, spear, or similar weapon. These soldiers formed a recognizable category in ancient armies, distinct from heavy infantry and archers.
3. In the Roman military context, these are men of the ranks intended to reinforce an official escort or a security detachment, as during Paul's transfer under good guard.
G1187.origine: The Greek word is composed of two elements: δεξιός ("right", "skilled") and λαμβάνω ("to take", "to seize"). The starting image is therefore that of someone who seizes with dexterity, especially with the right hand — a symbol of strength and mastery. A variant, δεξιοβόλος, uses βάλλω ("to throw") instead, giving the same meaning: an expert thrower. The word describes a specific military skill, that of the warrior capable of effectively wielding his weapon.
G1187.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 23:23, where the commander Claudius Lysias orders his men to prepare an escort to safely conduct Paul to Governor Felix. The military context is clear: different categories of soldiers (cavalry, lancers, light infantry) are enumerated to form an imposing procession intended to protect an important prisoner on the road. The Greek term used emphasizes the professional nature and equipment of these warriors.
G1187.portee: This word reminds us that the early Church lived under the protection of Roman law, even in the face of serious accusations. Paul benefits from an official and disciplined guard, affirming his status as a Roman citizen and reflecting God's providence: his enemies cannot harm him without the approval of the authorities. This detail of the narrative underscores divine sovereignty over the course of persecution.

sens: That which is located on the right side of the body, the side opposite to the left
The right hand, arm, or member on the right side
That which is done with the right hand or by the right side
Position of honor or power, at the right hand of someone
The right hand as a sign of alliance or association
Seat of Christ at the right hand of God, place of power and heavenly glory
G1188.detail:
1. The word "right" primarily designates what belongs to the right side of the body: in Matthew 5:29, Jesus speaks of "the right eye" as one of our members. It is the direction opposite to the left, a simple fact of body geography.
2. The right hand is mentioned repeatedly, as it was the preferred member for acting and fighting: Jesus says in Matthew 5:30 "your right hand", and John 18:10 recounts that the servant cut off "the right ear" of the high priest with his sword.
3. That which is done on the right side or with the right hand can designate the action itself: in 2 Corinthians 6:7, Paul refers to the "weapons of the right" to signify the offensive weapons held in the right (as opposed to defensive weapons on the left).
4. The "right" becomes a place of honor: in Matthew 20:21, the sons of Zebedee ask Jesus to sit "one at your right and the other at your left" in his kingdom — it is a position of proximity and power next to the sovereign.
5. Giving the "right hand" is a gesture of alliance and trust: in Galatians 2:9, James, Cephas, and John give "the hand" to Paul and Barnabas "of association", sealing their fraternal agreement.
6. The right hand of God is the supreme seat of the exalted Christ: in Matthew 26:64, Jesus announces that he will be seen "sitting at the right hand of the power of God", which expresses his glorious enthronement and limitless authority.
G1188.origine: The Greek word δεξιός comes from an ancient root meaning "skilled, apt to", as for most humans the right hand was (and remains) the dominant hand, that of skill and strength. In biblical Hebrew, יָמִין (yamin) carries the same meaning: "right" or "right hand", but it often also designates what is to the right as a sacred space or place of honor — a usage that Greek has adopted. The family of δεξιός includes δέξιος (to welcome), as the right hand is the one that receives or greets.
G1188.emploi: The word appears 54 times in the New Testament, mostly to designate the right side or member of the body (Matthew 5:29-30, John 18:10). Very often, it refers to the right hand as the seat of power or authority: Christ is seated "at the right hand" of God (Matthew 26:64, Mark 14:62, Luke 22:69, Acts 2:33), an image that underscores his cosmic dominion and participation in divine authority. The word is also used for places of honor within a community (Matthew 20:21) and for gestures of alliance (Galatians 2:9). In Revelation, John sees the "seven stars" in the "right hand" of the risen Christ (Revelation 1:16), a symbol of his sovereign mastery over the Church.
G1188.portee: This word invites us to contemplate the position of honor and power that Jesus occupies next to the Father. When the Bible says that Christ "sat at the right hand of God", it affirms that his work is complete, accepted, and that he truly reigns over the universe. This is a foundation of Christian confidence: the Christ who has conquered death and is exalted to the heavens intercedes for us and governs all things according to divine will. Understanding this image restores meaning to faith and prayer.

sens: To have a need for something for oneself
To ask something of someone
To plead with someone earnestly
To address a prayer to God
To intercede with God for someone else
G1189.detail:
1. The original meaning of the word is "to have a need," "to lack something": it conveys the idea of someone who feels a deficiency and seeks to fill it. When the leper says to Jesus, "I beg you, make me clean" (Luke 5:12), he expresses his urgent need.

2. From this arises the meaning of "to ask" or "to plead": the one who prays makes a request to someone else. When the father cries, "I beg you, look at my son" (Luke 9:38), he earnestly asks for Jesus' help.

3. "To plead" emphasizes the pressing, humble nature of the request, often mixed with emotion. The verb can express a sincere supplication and the destitution of the one who asks.

4. When it comes to praying to God, the word takes on its full spiritual dimension: it is addressing the Lord to express one's needs, trust, and desires. Cornelius "prayed to God continually" (Acts 10:2) in a constant attitude of piety.

5. Prayer can also be intercession: praying for someone else, bringing their needs before God. Paul asks the Romans to "pray" to the Lord for him (Romans 1:10), meaning to intercede for him with God.
G1189.origine: The word δέομαι comes from the verb δέω which fundamentally means "to have need" or "to lack." The starting image is that of someone who experiences a gap, a lack, and seeks to fill it by asking others. In Hebrew, it often translates חנן (favor, grace), which emphasizes that to pray is to ask for the favor, the grace of the one to whom one addresses. The word is common among classical Greek authors to express any form of urgent request.
G1189.emploi: The verb appears 22 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Acts. Particularly in Luke, it designates the supplications addressed to Jesus by the crowds: the leper (Luke 5:12), the possessed man (Luke 8:28), the heartbroken father (Luke 9:38). In Acts, the word is used for prayer addressed to God: Cornelius prays to God (Acts 10:2), Simon the magician pleads with Peter and John (Acts 8:24). In Paul, it is found for intercession: he asks the Romans to pray for him to the Lord (Romans 1:10). The word retains the idea of urgent need and trust in the one to whom one addresses.
G1189.portee: This word teaches us that to pray is first to recognize a lack, a need, and to turn to God or to the one who can help us. To pray is not a hollow formula; it is an attitude of humble and confident dependence. For the Christian, this means that coming to pray to God is to confess one's need and faith that God can respond. The word also invites to fraternal intercession: bringing the needs of others before the Lord is a powerful act of love.

sens: who is from the city of Derbe or belongs to it
G1190.detail: 1. It is an adjective meaning "from Derbe" or "inhabitant of Derbe." It designates people who come from this city. In Acts 20:4, it qualifies Gaius, a traveling companion of the apostle Paul, to indicate that he is a citizen or native of the city of Derbe in Asia Minor.
G1190.origine: This Greek word is formed from the name of the city of Derbe (Δέρβη) and the suffix -αῖος which, in Greek, is used to create adjectives meaning "belonging to" or "coming from." It is a common construction to indicate geographical origin or belonging to a place.
G1190.emploi: The adjective "from Derbe" appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 20:4, in the list of companions accompanying Paul on his journey to Jerusalem. It serves to identify Gaius as being from Derbe, an important city in the province of Galatia in Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey). This mention is set in the context of Paul's third missionary journey, where he sought to gather representatives of the churches he had founded.
G1190.portee: This term reminds us that the Gospel reached distant cities and that believers from various geographical origins joined the apostle Paul to support the cause of Christ. It illustrates the universal expansion of the early Church beyond Jerusalem.

sens: City of Lycaonia, in Asia Minor
Place where Paul and Barnabas take refuge and preach
Region visited during Paul's missionary journeys
G1191.detail:
1. Derbe is a city located in Lycaonia, a region in southern Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey). It is always mentioned alongside its neighbor Lystra, forming a pair of cities that Paul regularly visits.
2. After being stoned in Lystra, Paul takes refuge in Derbe with Barnabas (Acts 14:6, 20). It is a place of escape and safety where the Gospel can be proclaimed without immediate violence.
3. Derbe is a key stop in Paul's missionary journeys: he visits it during his first journey with Barnabas (Acts 14), and then during his second journey with Silas (Acts 16:1), where he meets Timothy.
G1191.origine: The Greek name Δέρβη (Derbē) transcribes a local toponym of Anatolian origin. The city was known in the Greco-Roman ancient world as an urban center in the mountainous region of Lycaonia.
G1191.emploi: Derbe appears three times in Acts, always in the context of Paul's missionary journeys. Paul takes refuge there after being stoned in Lystra (Acts 14:6, 20), where he preaches and establishes the Church. He returns there during his second journey (Acts 16:1), where he finds Timothy, a disciple from the region. Thus, Derbe marks the geographical and spiritual stages of the spread of the Gospel in Asia Minor and Paul's pastoral ministry among the new churches.
G1191.portee: Derbe reminds us that the Lord opens paths of escape and places of refuge for His persecuted servants, and that the Gospel progresses even when opposition is violent. The mention of Timothy in Derbe shows how local converts become workers of the Kingdom, perpetuating the ministry of the Gospel from one generation to the next.

sens: The skin or hide of an animal, particularly that of sheep and goats
The garment made from this material
G1192.detail:
1. The word literally refers to the skin of an animal, its outer covering – here that of sheep and goats. It is a concrete term that refers to the raw material, before it is processed. In Hebrews 11:37, it specifically refers to these animal skins.
2. By extension, it refers to the garment made from this tanned skin that has become leather: it is the coat or tunic worn. The prophets and believers persecuted in biblical times wore such coarse garments, symbolizing their poverty and renunciation.
G1192.origine: The Greek word comes from a root meaning "to flay" or "to strip away." It translates the Hebrew עוֹר (ôr), which has the same meaning. This term belongs to a family of Greek words related to leather work and the outer covering of things. It is a simple and direct word, without particular connotation.
G1192.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 11:37. The context is that of a famous passage about the witnesses of faith in the Old Testament: the author lists the sufferings endured by these faithful men and women of God. Among them is the fact of being "clothed in skins of sheep and skins of goats." These rudimentary garments embody the destitution and voluntary misery accepted to remain faithful to God – an image of sacrifice and humiliation.
G1192.portee: This word reminds us that faithfulness to God comes at a cost: the believers of the Old Testament endured cold, poverty, and shame, clothed in rags. For the Christian reader, it is an invitation not to fear deprivation or the world's scorn if it means remaining attached to the faith. The image of animal skins transformed into garments also speaks of the grace that covers our human fragility.

sens: Made from animal skin
Clothing or accessory made from processed animal skin
G1193.detail:
1. The word "leather" refers to a material obtained by processing the skin of an animal: it is tanned and prepared skin that becomes solid and durable. In the Bible, leather is a valuable and common material, used for belts, sandals, wineskins, and many other everyday items.
2. By extension, the word applies to objects made from this material. John the Baptist wore "a leather belt around his waist" (Matthew 3:4), which shows the common use of leather in clothing, especially among those who lived simply or outdoors.
G1193.origine: The Greek word δερμάτινος comes from the noun δέρμα (derma), which means "skin." The suffix -ινος (-inos) creates an adjective indicating the material: "made of" or "crafted from." In Hebrew, this word generally corresponds to עוֹר (ôr), which refers both to the skin of a living being and the raw material processed into leather. It is a simple example of how the Greeks described materials.
G1193.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament, exclusively in the parallel passages of Matthew and Mark that describe John the Baptist's attire. These two identical verses recount that John wore a leather belt around his waist, a humble and practical accessory characteristic of someone living in the desert away from urban comforts. Leather is presented as a sober and durable element, suitable for the austere life of the prophet.
G1193.portee: The mention of leather in John the Baptist's clothing helps us understand that the essence of his ministry was not in appearance or comfort, but in the message of repentance he proclaimed. Leather, an ordinary and crafted material, symbolizes the authenticity and simplicity of one who does not seek to attract by appearance, but by the word of God.

sens: To flay, remove the skin from an animal
To strike someone repeatedly, to beat up
To maltreat, to treat violently
G1194.detail: 1. The original meaning is to flay or strip the skin from an animal — this is the primary image of the Greek word. The Greek Old Testament uses it to describe the preparation of sacrifices. 2. By extension, it means to strike someone violently and repeatedly, to beat mercilessly. The vineyard workers beat the master's servants (Matthew 21:35), and the Jewish authorities had the apostles beaten with rods (Acts 5:40): in all these cases, it involves repeated strikes, often public and humiliating. 3. In a figurative or intensified sense, it means to maltreat, to treat with brutality. Paul says he treats his body "by beating it" to bring it into subjection (1 Corinthians 9:26), or speaks of receiving blows to the face (2 Corinthians 11:20): this is not an isolated blow, but maltreatment.
G1194.origine: The verb δέρω comes from a root meaning first "to flay" or "to strip" — the image is that of removing skin. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, the same meaning is found in related words: Leviticus describes the dismemberment of sacrificial animals. From this concrete and brutal sense — to tear away, to strip — the word has extended to mean to strike and beat.
G1194.emploi: The verb appears about fifteen times in the New Testament, mostly in Luke, and concentrated in three contexts. First, the parable of the vineyard workers: the master's servants are beaten, one after another (Matthew 21:35, Mark 12:3, 5, Luke 20:10, 11). Next, the passion of Jesus: he is struck in the face by those holding him (Luke 22:63, John 18:23). Finally, the persecution of the apostles: the authorities have them beaten with rods (Acts 5:40, 16:37, 22:19). Paul also uses the word in the sense of disciplining the body (1 Corinthians 9:26) or receiving blows (2 Corinthians 11:20). The word always denotes real physical violence, never purely moral punishment.
G1194.portee: This verb reminds the reader that physical violence against the servants of God — whether against the prophets of the Old Testament or the apostles — is a constant motif of the rejection of the Gospel. It also emphasizes that the suffering of the believer can be bodily, real, like that of Jesus and the early disciples, and that faith at that time came at a price of blood.

sens: to chain, imprison
to attach, fix together
to load, impose a burden
G1195.detail:
1. To put someone in chains or to hold them prisoner: it is to immobilize a person to control or punish them. When Paul recounts his past, he says he "bound" believers to throw them in prison (Acts 22:4) — he physically tied them up before imprisoning them.
2. To attach, assemble, or fix things together to make a whole. The scribes "bind" burdens (Matthew 23:4): they gather them into tight packages.
3. By extension, to load someone with a moral weight or an oppressive obligation: "to bind a burden on the shoulders" means to impose a difficult load on someone without helping them.
G1195.origine: The word comes from δεσμός (desmos), which means "link, chain, prison." It is the same word found in "desert" (a place where one is bound by isolation) and in other Greek words referring to what binds or holds. In the Old Testament, it primarily translates the Hebrew words for "to bind" or "to chain" (אָסַר and אָלַם).
G1195.emploi: The verb appears three times in the New Testament. It first denotes the action of putting someone in chains or in prison (Luke 8:29, where a possessed man was "bound" to control him; Acts 22:4, where Paul imprisoned Christians). It also describes the action of binding together, assembling, or attaching — notably the burdens imposed by the scribes on the people (Matthew 23:4). The meaning varies between the physical and concrete action (chaining a person) and the moral or figurative action (imposing a burden).
G1195.portee: This word helps the reader grasp the violence of chains — physical or moral — that bind men. When Jesus commands the demon to release the man, or when Paul acknowledges his past as a persecutor, the word "bind" returns to the real weight of oppression. For the scribes who "bind" burdens, the word denounces hypocrisy: loading others with rules without helping them. It is a call to see in true faith not new chains, but liberation.

sens: Bundle of grains or plants tied together
G1197.detail: 1. A sheaf is a collection of stalks of wheat, barley, or other grain gathered and tied together after the harvest. The word paints the concrete image of the work of harvesters: they cut the plants, gather them, and bind them. In Jesus' parable in Matthew 13:30, he speaks of binding the tares into sheaves to be burned, while the good wheat is gathered into the barn — two opposing destinies marked by the very form of the word, which emphasizes the unity and solidarity of things gathered together.
G1197.origine: The word δέσμη comes from the verb δέω (déô, "to bind"). The noun literally designates what is bound or what binds. In ancient Hebrew, the corresponding word אֲגֻדָּה (agoudah) has the same meaning: a bundle or a sheaf of things gathered and tied together. The same root δέσμη will also produce the word δεσμά (desmá, "bonds," "chains"), which extends the idea of constraint and binding.
G1197.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 13:30, in the parable of the good grain and the tares. Jesus describes the work of the harvesters: they bind the tares into separate sheaves to destroy them by fire, while the wheat is gathered into the barn. This agricultural context is the natural backdrop of the word — every ancient reader, especially in Palestine, knew this common practice and immediately recognized the image. The word emphasizes that the tares and the wheat, although mixed in growth, are ultimately separated and distinctly bound before their final judgment.
G1197.portee: This image of the sheaf helps the reader understand the final judgment: God does not destroy the wicked randomly, but with order and intention. Furthermore, the parable teaches that patience and waiting until the harvest are necessary — one cannot judge or act too soon. For the believer, this image also evokes the security of gathering: the good wheat will be bound and safely gathered, like a protected sheaf.

sens: One who is held captive, chained by authority
One who is imprisoned for a crime or accusation
Figuratively: one who is spiritually bound to Christ or to His cause
G1198.detail:
1. The word primarily designates someone who is physically bound or held captive. In Roman times, it referred to a man kept under lock and key, whom the governor could release as an act of grace during a festival (Matthew 27:15). The jailer in Philippi kept these men locked up, ready to watch over them (Acts 16:27).
2. More specifically, it refers to a person arrested and imprisoned for a legal reason: Paul himself, after his arrest in Jerusalem, became a prisoner in the hands of the Romans (Acts 28:17). Festus speaks of Paul as a prisoner left by his predecessor (Acts 25:14).
3. Paul uses this word figuratively to describe his spiritual condition: he calls himself a "prisoner in the Lord" (Ephesians 4:1) and a "prisoner of Jesus Christ" (Ephesians 3:1, 2 Timothy 1:8). It is no longer about physical chains, but being completely bound to Christ and His service, which paradoxically is true freedom for the believer.
G1198.origine: The word comes from the root "desmos" (link, chain). A prisoner is literally someone who is bound, chained. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, the equivalent is "asir," which carries the same imagery: one who is held, attached. This root reminds us that ancient imprisonment was primarily a matter of physical bonds rather than a closed structure.
G1198.emploi: The word appears 17 times in the New Testament, mainly in the accounts of Acts and in Paul's epistles. In the Gospels (Matthew, Mark), it refers to ordinary prisoners whom the governor released each year, notably Barabbas. In Acts, the context broadens: Paul speaks of the prisoners locked up in Philippi (16:25, 16:27), and we see how Paul himself transitions from the status of a free apostle to that of a political prisoner in Jerusalem and Rome (25:14, 28:17). The usage becomes theologically rich when Paul refers to himself as a "prisoner of Christ" or "prisoner in the Lord" (Ephesians 3:1, 4:1, 2 Timothy 1:8, Philemon 1:9), reversing the meaning: his legal captivity is in reality a joyful imprisonment in the service of the Gospel. The epistle to the Hebrews also speaks of sympathy towards prisoners (10:34, 13:3).
G1198.portee: This word sheds light on how Paul understands his suffering. Chained for preaching Christ, he does not complain: he sees his imprisonment as a complete belonging to Christ. For the Christian reader, this teaches that the limitations imposed by the world can become opportunities to witness and to depend entirely on God. The New Testament exhortations to remember prisoners (Hebrews 13:3) remind us that supporting those who suffer for Christ is a mark of communion with Him.

sens: That which physically binds or holds: chain, restraint, cord
Captivity, imprisonment: the state of a chained prisoner
That which binds morally or spiritually: obligation, attachment, dependence
Restriction, figurative restraint: that which immobilizes or limits freedom
G1199.detail:
1. In a concrete sense, the link is the material object that holds someone: chain, restraints on feet or hands. Luke 8:29 describes a possessed man who was kept "bound with chains," as he had the strength to break them. It is the physical instrument of captivity.
2. By extension, the word designates captivity itself, the state of imprisonment. When Paul speaks of his "bonds" (Acts 26:29; Philippians 1:7), he evokes both the concrete chains and the fact of being a prisoner, arrested.
3. Spiritually or morally, "link" means that which unites or binds internally: a moral obligation, an attachment, a dependence. Paul says that the brothers "share in the same grace" with him in his bonds (Philippians 1:7), suggesting a deep communion.
4. The link can also be an infirmity or an imposed limit: Mark 7:35 speaks of the "bond of the tongue," the impediment that prevented a deaf man from speaking clearly — an invisible but real restraint.
G1199.origine: The Greek word desmos comes from the verb "deo" (to bind, to tie). It is a concrete word of origin: it evokes the action of binding something or someone with a rope or chain. In ancient Hebrew, it is often found translating the word "assar" (to attach, to bind). The family includes other words related to binding and captivity, all built on this root of the verb to bind.
G1199.emploi: The word "link" appears 18 times in the New Testament, especially in Acts and Paul's epistles. In Acts, it first refers to the physical chains of prisoners (Acts 16:26, 22:30). But in Paul, particularly in Philippians and Philemon, the meaning broadens: his "bonds" (his captivity) become a sign of his faithfulness to Christ and even an occasion for testimony (Philippians 1:13-14). Hebrews 11:36 and Jude 1:6 also use it for spiritual chains. Mark 7:35 uses the word figuratively for a physical restraint (the bond of the tongue). Thus, the Bible gradually transitions from material bonds to moral or spiritual attachments.
G1199.portee: For the believer, this word reveals that physical captivity does not stop the Gospel: Paul, chained, continues to proclaim Christ and encourages the brothers (Philippians 1:12-14). It also shows that some spiritual bonds — infirmities, dependencies, limitations — can be broken by Christ, like the unclean spirit that bound the man in Luke 8:29. It is an invitation to recognize where we are bound and to seek our freedom in Him.
